articles.title: Twitter makes stock symbol $ ‘cashtag’ links official, following # and @
articles.summary: Now another common standard will automatically be turned into links when viewed on Twitter.com - $ stock symbols. Twitter announced it in a tweet that indeed contains a stock link that is clickable on the web, much as it has been on various Twitter clients before today. Clicking on a ticker link takes you to a straight Twitter search for the symbol.
articles.body: Twitter has a long history of letting its users create standards and then finally adopting them as site features. First came the @ reply, whose history was recently examined. Next, the # hashtag morphed into Twitter’s full “Discover” tab — complete with advertising opportunities. Now another common standard will automatically be turned into links when viewed on Twitter.com - $ stock symbols, commonly referred to as “cashtags.” Twitter announced it in a tweet that indeed contains a stock link that is clickable on the web, much as it has been on various Twitter clients before today. Clicking on a ticker link takes you to a straight Twitter search for the symbol. Twitter has been working to make its website better at showing related information in “expanded Tweets” that, in part, make it so a user doesn’t need to leave Twitter.com. While the tweets with stock ticker symbols don’t yet show expanded information, we imagine that it’s an obvious opportunity to do so.

articles.title: Mamdani says wealthy donors killed California’s billionaire tax — but Americans aren't done forcing the rich to pay up
articles.summary: "There were other ballot referendums that took place across the country calling for what is essentially the same thing."
articles.body:
California voters may have rejected a one-time tax on billionaires, but New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said that vote alone tells us little about how Americans feel about taxing the rich.

Speaking at The New York Times' DealBook Summit on Nov. 22, Mamdani said opponents spent heavily to defeat Proposition 40 in California. He then pointed to other states where voters approved higher taxes on wealthy people.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 5 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

"There were other ballot referendums that took place across the country calling for what is essentially the same thing, which is higher taxes on the wealthiest," Mamdani said, according to the Times .

In New York, the democratic socialist mayor has clashed with some of Wall Street's biggest names over his own push to raise taxes on wealthy New Yorkers.

California's Proposition 40 would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of residents worth more than $1 billion, with most of the money going to healthcare. The measure lost with 52% of voters voting against it.

One committee fighting the tax raised more than $333 million, with major donations from Google co-founder Sergey Brin and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. Gov. Gavin Newsom also opposed the measure.

Critics, meanwhile, warned that it could drive billionaires out of California and cost the state income tax revenue. California's top 1% of earners paid nearly 37% of the state's personal income taxes in 2023, according to the governor's 2026–27 budget summary.

"I don't think you're going to see such a good Democratic electorate in the near future," Wesley Hussey, a political science professor at California State University in Sacramento, told the Associated Press . "This was the time to pass something that was pretty lefty and progressive and had a lot of opposition."

In New York, Mamdani took his case for taxing the rich straight to the front door of one of the wealthiest people in the city. "Well, today, we're taxing the rich," Mamdani said in a video filmed outside the Manhattan building where hedge fund billionaire Ken Griffin owns a penthouse.

articles.title: Motociclistas que dão grau e postam na internet são alvos de operação | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo o Ministério Público, grupo usava redes sociais para divulgar, promover e incentivar manobras. Armas, celulares, munições e motos também foram apreendidos.
articles.summary: Operação contra grau no ES prende três em flagrante e suspende 16 habilitações após investigação de manobras perigosas divulgadas em redes sociais em Linhares.
articles.body:
Três pessoas são presas em operação que investiga suspeitos de manobras irregulares com motocicletas no Espírito Santo — Foto: Divulgação/MPES

Três pessoas foram presas em flagrante durante uma operação voltada ao combate de manobras perigosas com motocicletas, conhecidas como "grau", em Linhares , no Norte do Espírito Santo, na manhã desta terça-feira (24).

Além das prisões, foram apreendidos celulares, armas, munições, motos, peças automotivas, materiais de divulgação e troféus utilizados em manobras.

Ao todo, 16 mandados de busca e apreensão foram cumpridos. Segundo o Ministério Público do Espírito Santo (MPES), o grupo usava redes sociais para divulgar, promover e incentivar as manobras.

De acordo com as investigações, desenvolvidas a partir do setor de Inteligência da Guarda Civil Municipal de Linhares, foram identificados indícios da atuação recorrente e articulada de motociclistas na realização de manobras de risco.

A Justiça do Espírito Santo deferiu medidas cautelares de suspensão da permissão ou da habilitação para dirigir, além da suspensão das redes sociais utilizadas para a divulgação das manobras. Segundo balanço do MPES, 16 motociclistas tiveram a habilitação suspensa e 18 perfis nas redes sociais serão derrubados.

A operação abrange investigados nos municípios de Linhares, Sooretama e São Gabriel da Palha , também no Norte do estado. As idades e nomes dos detidos não foram divulgados.

Para chegar aos suspeitos, foi feita uma análise de imagens do sistema de videomonitoramento municipal e de redes sociais. A partir desse monitoramento, foi possível identificar condutores, motocicletas e perfis digitais utilizados para as práticas.

Durante as diligências, também foram identificadas motocicletas com modificações irregulares, como escapamentos adulterados, ausência de retrovisores e dispositivos destinados a dificultar a identificação das placas.

Para o MPES, além de elementos para o esclarecimento dos fatos e a eventual responsabilização dos envolvidos, a atuação tem caráter preventivo, contribuindo para a proteção das pessoas que utilizam as vias da região.

As condutas investigadas podem caracterizar crimes previstos no Código de Trânsito Brasileiro, sem prejuízo da apuração de outras infrações.

articles.title: Coast Guard boards 2 foreign ships bound for US amid reports of Iranian hacking probe
articles.summary: U.S. Coast Guard cyber teams boarded two foreign vessels in the Gulf of America after their networks were compromised by foreign cyber actors at sea.
articles.body: The U.S. Coast Guard deployed specialized cyber teams to board two foreign-flagged commercial ships bound for U.S. ports in August after indications that their networks had been compromised by "foreign cyber actors," a Coast Guard spokesperson told Fox News Digital on Monday. The offshore operations took place Aug. 21 and 24 in the Gulf of America, with teams mitigating the threats before the vessels reached U.S. ports. The confirmation came as The Wall Street Journal also reported Monday that U.S. authorities are investigating whether Iran was involved in dozens of cyberattacks targeting energy tankers. FEARS OF CHINA SPYING ON US MILITARY PROMPT GOP HAWKS TO DEMAND RETALIATION AGAINST THE SHIPPING GIANT "The U.S. Coast Guard (USCG), in close coordination with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and federal cybersecurity experts, recently conducted joint offshore security boardings of two inbound foreign-flagged commercial vessels in the Gulf of America," a Coast Guard spokesperson said. "The measures were designed to ensure the integrity of the vessel’s operational and information technology systems following indications that the networks of both vessels were compromised by foreign cyber actors." The Coast Guard said a specialized team of law enforcement personnel, Coast Guard Cyber Protection Team members, a vessel inspector and FBI Cyber Action Team operators boarded the first vessel Aug. 21 to investigate the suspected cybersecurity breach. "The captain, crew and shore-side corporate staff were critical partners in helping to ensure the threats were mitigated," the spokesperson added. A similar multiagency boarding and safety verification operation was conducted Aug. 24 aboard the second vessel, also in the Gulf of America, the Coast Guard said. FRENCH SUPERMARKETS FACE MILLIONS IN LOSSES AFTER CYBERATTACK HITS REFRIGERATORS NATIONWIDE No operational disruptions, vessel instability, threats to crew safety or environmental impacts have been reported. The Coast Guard said it is coordinating with port operators, vessel owners and local maritime stakeholders to ensure port operations continue safely and without interruption. According to The Wall Street Journal, attackers exploited vulnerabilities in Fortinet networking equipment, prompting Coast Guard boardings after crews received bomb threats warning that "traitor ships will burn in hell." STRAIT OF HORMUZ CRISIS TRAPS 6,000 SAILORS AS ATTACKS ON SHIPS MOUNT, UN MARITIME CHIEF SAYS As many as 50 vessels carrying oil, liquefied petroleum, chemicals and other potentially explosive cargo are believed to have been targeted, the outlet reported, citing U.S. officials. A European shipping executive also said officers received threats on their cellphones. A ransom letter addressed to the captain of the Liberian-flagged supertanker Prosperity, which was carrying about 2.3 million barrels of oil, described the operation as a "planned execution." Hackers reportedly breached one vessel's propulsion and navigation systems, disrupting communications for about 30 hours and forcing the crew to switch to manual procedures, potentially delaying energy shipments to Asia and Europe. AMERICA MUST DEFEND OUR DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE, HERE AND OVERSEAS, TO WIN THE NEXT WAR "The Marine Transportation System is vital to America's economic prosperity and national security, and safeguarding it against potential cyber risks is a standard part of the United States Coast Guard's safety and security mission," the Coast Guard spokesperson said. "Just as we monitor for mechanical or weather-related hazards, we incorporate cyber risk management into our routine, professional approach to facilitating commerce and ensuring safe vessel transits into and from our ports and waterways. "While confirmed cyber disruptions in the maritime domain remain uncommon, even isolated technical issues can cause avoidable commercial delays. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We encourage all maritime stakeholders to leverage Coast Guard Cyber Command’s free, non-regulatory technical resources to maintain strong digital hygiene and report any suspected anomalies to the National Response Center," the spokesperson added.

articles.title: Army wants to resume helicopter flights near Reagan National airport
articles.summary: The Army is seeking federal approval to resume helicopter training flights near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, drawing safety concerns nearly two years after a deadly midair collision over the Potomac River killed 67 people. Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), whose district includes the airport, said Monday that Army officials informed his office during a briefing…
articles.body:
The Army is seeking federal approval to resume helicopter training flights near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, drawing safety concerns nearly two years after a deadly midair collision over the Potomac River killed 67 people.

Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), whose district includes the airport, said Monday that Army officials informed his office during a briefing that they had contacted the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) about restarting the flights and were awaiting a response.

“Army officials assured my office that no flights will take place unless they are approved by the FAA,” Beyer wrote in a post on the social platform X . “While Army officials further committed to implementing all NTSB [National Transportation Safety Board] safety recommendations, it is clear that this work is not complete.”

He continued, “The path forward must prioritize safety, and that requires full implementation of the NTSB’s recommendations before training flights resume.”

An Army spokesperson told Politico on Monday that the military hopes to restart the flights as early as the second week of December. Army officials also briefed staff on the Senate Commerce and Armed Services committees last week, according to the outlet.

The FAA told Politico on Friday that it had not received a formal request to restart the flights and reiterated Monday that the Army would need the agency’s approval before training could resume.

Federal regulators imposed restrictions on helicopter traffic near Reagan National Airport near Washington, D.C., after an Army Black Hawk helicopter collided with an American Airlines regional passenger jet in January 2025, killing everyone aboard both aircrafts.

The FAA suspended military helicopter training flights in the area in May of that year after another Black Hawk flew too close to the airport, prompting air traffic controllers to divert commercial flights.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called the incident “unacceptable” at the time and vowed to press Pentagon officials on “why the hell our rules were disregarded.”

Lawmakers announced a practical agreement on aviation safety legislation intended to prevent another deadly collision. Negotiations have centered in part on requirements for military aircrafts to use surveillance technology that would improve pilots’ awareness of any nearby aircrafts.

The Army’s own investigation into the fatal collision produced more than 30 recommendations, including changes to air traffic control procedures and better coordination with the FAA.

articles.title: Army proceeding with lead detonation on Wednesday
articles.summary: The Army is going ahead with detonating lead-containing munitions in Iowa on Wednesday after President Trump threw additional uncertainty into the controversy on Monday. “We are proceeding with the controlled removal in full coordination with all state, local and federal authorities, because the safety of Iowa’s citizens comes first,” said acting Army Secretary Adam Telle…
articles.body:
The Army is going ahead with detonating lead-containing munitions in Iowa on Wednesday after President Trump threw additional uncertainty into the controversy on Monday.

“We are proceeding with the controlled removal in full coordination with all state, local and federal authorities, because the safety of Iowa’s citizens comes first,” said acting Army Secretary Adam Telle in a post on X.

Telle said moving forward was a “consensus decision.”

“Every expert agency agrees, and both Iowa’s current and incoming Governors say the call belongs to the experts,” he wrote, also noting that a federal appeals court declined to block an emergency permit for controlled explosion on Monday.

The Army announced last week that it planned to detonate degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, in a matter of days — resulting in a plume with lead-containing particles in the air.

The announcement created an uproar, causing fears that people would be exposed to toxic lead both immediately and in the aftermath. The federal government has argued that doing a controlled detonation would be more favorable than risking an accidental explosion. The saga has also raised questions about why the situation is happening in the first place.

The detonation had been slated for Monday, but on Sunday, the Army said it would actually be postponed until Wednesday “to allow for more optimal weather conditions.”

However, Trump on Monday said the Army would only go ahead with agreement from the court and Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D).

Sand later said that the administration should make the decision.

In children, exposure to lead can cause brain damage, nervous system damage, learning problems, behavioral issues and a lower IQ. In rare cases, it can also cause seizures, coma and death, according to the Environmental Protection Agency.

In adults, lead exposure can cause decreased kidney function, heart-related issues and fertility issues.

articles.title: AI market whipsaw puts Kevin Warsh's rate-hike strategy to the test
articles.summary: With Warsh silent during the market's recent swings, investors are parsing both the divided commentary from his colleagues and the clues he left behind at hi...
articles.body:
When stocks tanked last week, Wall Street briefly bet the Federal Reserve would ease up on interest rate hikes. Now Monday's massive rebound — sparked by Jensen Huang's reinstatement at Nvidia — has revived bets on at least two more interest rate hikes.

Yet with AI stocks still off their highs, the sector's volatility is emerging as a critical test for Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh and the central bank's path for rate hikes.

"AI stress is not mostly due to the Fed. But it is not a coincidence it is occurring when the Fed is hiking," said Krishna Guha, head of central banking and the economy for Evercore ISI. "Talk of 50-basis-point hikes or faster tightening adds to stress. Fed Chair Warsh not talking is a problem. It leaves the market guessing: Is he a hardcore hawk or a market-sensitive hawk? The gap is filled by others whose views can lag the leadership."

"This is a serious test for Warsh," Guha added.

With Warsh silent during the market's recent swings, investors are parsing both the divided commentary from his colleagues and the clues he left behind at his late-October press conference.

Last week, Fed officials offered competing visions for how aggressively to move. Fed governor Chris Waller said that if the central bank hikes by a quarter point next month, it will need to signal a follow-up hike of the same size in January — or else deliver a jumbo half-percentage-point increase in December . Fed governor Lisa Cook echoed that urgency on Friday, right as the market hit its nadir. Arguing that financial conditions remain too accommodative while inflation stays stubbornly high, she warned the central bank risks falling behind the curve if it doesn't hike now.

New York Fed president John Williams, however, pushed back against calls for supersize rate hikes , saying last week that he doesn't think the situation calls for "dramatic action."

For his part, Warsh staked out a middle-ground framework following the Fed's decision to hold rates steady on Oct. 28 — three-and-a-half weeks before the tech rout. While noting that overall financial and credit conditions had tightened since September's rate hike, he stopped short of calling them "tight." Crucially, he also signaled he is watching the AI sector closely , noting that credit spreads had widened for certain assets and acknowledging that interest rates are not "somehow divorced" from the AI investment surge.

Now, Wall Street is divided over whether Warsh's focus on financial conditions will restrain the central bank, or if his inflation target will force him to keep hiking into a fragile market.

articles.title: Too young to be vaccinated for measles? Babies face growing threats from outbreaks
articles.summary: As measles outbreaks continue to soar, a new question has emerged: Should doctors give measles shots earlier to better protect babies?
articles.body:
As measles outbreaks continue to soar nationwide, increasingly spilling from small, close-knit communities into the general population, a new question has emerged: Should doctors give measles shots earlier to better protect babies?

Dr. Kristen Panthagani, an emergency medicine doctor in Connecticut, is worried about her baby, who has just turned 6 months old — too young for the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine that's given after age 1.

"I've been trying to figure out what to do to protect my son," Panthagani said on her public health blog, called " You can know things ." He's "in a tricky period when it comes to measles. He's in a window of vulnerability where he likely doesn't have protection against the virus."

Babies are born with antibodies against measles if their mothers have been vaccinated. But new evidence shows that protection doesn't last as long as previously thought.

"The assumption has always been that up until 6 months of age, babies are protected, and then from 6 to 12 months, there's some waning," said Dr. Buddy Creech, a pediatric infectious disease specialist and director of the Vanderbilt Vaccine Research Program at Vanderbilt University Medical Center. "That's why we give the vaccine at 12 months."

New research from Creech's team shows that protection is gone long before a child's first birthday. Researchers analyzed blood samples from 92 mother-infant pairs and found that less than 20% of 6-month-old babies still have those protective antibodies.

"By somewhere between 4 to 6 months of age, the majority of kids have completely lost the level of seroprotection that would be needed to protect against measles," Creech said. He presented the research at an October meeting of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. It's not been peer-reviewed.

For more on the measles outbreak, read The Vaccine Divide , a data investigation into how the deadly virus is roaring back and childhood vaccine defenses continue to crack and crumble.

Now that cases have exploded in the U.S., babies in that 6- to 11-month window are increasingly defenseless against the virus.

"We're going to have to rethink when we should give the first dose of measles vaccine," Creech said.

When should kids get their measles shots?

For decades, the guidance was straightforward: Children receive their first MMR shot at 12 to 15 months old, followed by a second dose between ages 4 and 6. Together, the shots are 97% effective at protecting against measles, usually for life.

In areas with active outbreaks, however, babies at 6 months old can get an early or "zero" MMR shot ahead of their two regular doses.

And toddlers who've already had their first regular dose don't have to wait until age 4 for their second shot. They're eligible for the second dose 28 days after their first for maximum protection.

Many parents in outbreak areas have taken advantage of the change in guidance. "We have seen huge uptake in the zero dose as well as in the early second dose," Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Dr. Debra Bogen said last week during a briefing with the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials. More than 67,000 early MMR shots have been given in Pennsylvania since July, according to the state health department .

The growing question now is whether those exceptions should become more widely used — or whether the routine vaccination schedule itself needs reconsideration — now that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status.

"There are people looking at this right now. They're reviewing all of the latest science and seeing if the recommendation should change," said Dr. Deanna Behrens, a Chicago-area pediatrician and secretary of the Illinois chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics. "We are on high alert."

As of Friday, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had confirmed 5,838 cases , though the number is likely a vast undercount. More than 1,000 of those cases have been in kids under 5. About 17% of those children have needed hospitalization.

Most kids recover from measles without a problem. But as the virus has caught fire across the U.S., doctors in outbreak zones have reported severe complications in some children , including trouble breathing, severe dehydration, pneumonia and brain swelling. Babies with measles are also at greater risk of developing a condition called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE, years after their infection. It's almost always fatal.

Twelve people have died of measles this year, according to state health departments. At least half of those deaths have been in babies or toddlers.

The Vaccine Integrity Project, part of the University of Minnesota's Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy, recently summarized the latest data on zero doses of MMR vaccine. The shot is 58% effective when given between 6 and 9 months, and 83% between 9 and 11 months.

Side effects from the shots, such as fever and, rarely, febrile seizures, were the same in younger and older children.

But there's also evidence, the Vaccine Integrity Project's review found, that the zero dose may impact how well kids' immune systems respond to the two routinely recommended MMR shots.

"It's a trade-off right now," said Dr. Heidi Moline, a pediatrician and clinical adviser to the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy. "When there's a significant amount of measles virus circulating, the short-term benefit of protection against measles outweighs the long-term lower antibodies."

As of now, there's no indication the CDC is considering changes to the childhood vaccine schedule. The AAP said the group will review all of its immunization recommendations early next year. The CDC didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Vaccines recommended by the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices are generally free. There have been reports of health insurance claims being denied for early MMR vaccination, according to the AAP.

"This is something the vaccine policy people are really going to have to look at," said Dr. Peter Hotez, co-director of the Texas Children's Hospital Center for Vaccine Development.

articles.title: TSA detects suspicious movement in traveler’s suitcase during security screening
articles.summary: A TSA officer at Ontario International Airport spotted suspicious movement in a traveler's luggage and found live snakes, including a rattlesnake, inside a checked bag. An expert weighed in.
articles.body: TSA officers at California’s Ontario International Airport (ONT) recently faced an alarming situation while screening a checked bag. During a routine bag inspection, TSA Officer Benjamin Andrade-Carillo spotted suspicious movement in a pillowcase. Initially, the shape inside the pillowcase appeared stringy, like a rope. But on closer inspection, the officer saw that the object was moving, according to an employee story published on the agency’s website. TSA OFFICER SEES ALARMING SHAPES ON X-RAY BEFORE STOLEN CIVIL WAR MYSTERY UNRAVELS The officer removed the pillowcase from the bag and quickly determined it was not rope. "When I realized the item in my hand was alive, I told myself, ‘I need to escalate this immediately,’" Andrade-Carillo said, the TSA's website noted. Andrade-Carillo notified his supervisory officer, Suggey Flores. "I felt it tense up and start moving," Flores said. SHARP WEAPON DISCOVERED BY TSA TUCKED INSIDE UNUSUAL ITEM IN PASSENGER'S CARRY-ON BAG "I have held snakes before, so I wasn’t too spooked. I was more impressed," he added, "because it’s not something you see every day." Flores informed the ONT TSA manager, Francisco "Frank" Calderon, as well as airport police and the airline about the find. Calderon confirmed there were live snakes inside the pillowcase and that one was a rattlesnake. "TSA officers should not be handling live snakes for safety reasons," Calderon said. "Our priority was ensuring the safety of our officers and everyone in the area while making the proper notifications and coordinating a safe resolution," according to the TSA. "I felt it tense up and start moving." Due to safety reasons, the immediate area was vacated. "Safety was a concern because we didn’t know what kind of snakes they were," Flores said. "They could have been venomous." BIZARRE X-RAY SCAN LEADS TSA OFFICERS TO FLIGHT PASSENGER'S ILLEGAL STASH The flyer removed the snakes and gave them to a non-traveling family member. TSA then re-screened the luggage and permitted the traveler to fly. Fox News Digital reached out to the agency for more information. "The transportation of live reptiles is not automatically prohibited, but acceptance of venomous species is much more restrictive for airlines," Keith Jeffries of Florida, vice president of K2 Security Screening Group and a former federal security director for TSA at Los Angeles International Airport, told Fox News Digital. The traveler said the snakes were pets, according to the Los Angeles TSA Coordination Center. He also said he had previously traveled with the snakes on another airline. "I've seen cases with birds, turtles, snakes. I mean, it's just never-ending." "The basic rule is you need to [give] plenty of advance notice if you're shipping those types of items," said Jeffries. "You have got to have the proper containers. You've got to have the warning labels, the documentation for the permits to transport it." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER He went on, "Then, of course, you've got to have somebody that specializes in handling that type of cargo that's properly trained. They look for the environmental conditions and the safe loading and unloading of those types of animals." "In my two years of service, I had not found anything like this," Andrade-Carillo said in the employee story on the TSA site. "In San Diego, I experienced a gentleman trying to bring live lobsters as a carry-on." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES "We ask the traveling public to be mindful of what they bring in their bags," he also said, "because if we don’t know what it is, we will find out." "I am very happy with the way our team handled the situation, stopped screening when they needed to and made the proper notifications," Calderon said. "No injuries or bites were reported, thank goodness." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Jason Pantages, the TSA’s federal security director for Los Angeles International and surrounding airports, agreed with that assessment. "This incident demonstrates the sound judgment and teamwork of the ONT TSA workforce as well as the importance of travelers checking with their airline before bringing animals, including reptiles, to the airport," said Pantages on the TSA's site. "I've seen cases with birds, turtles, snakes before. I mean, it's just never-ending," Jeffries told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It's not that they're trying to wreak havoc on a security system," he added. At times, flyers are just "trying to make a buck. It's [as] simple as that."

articles.title: Bill Ackman says the U.S. economy could be headed for another recession—and is blaming Kevin Warsh’s Fed
articles.summary: “The Fed will put the U.S. and [the] world in recession if it continues to raise rates in a failed attempt to drive inflation to 2%,” Ackman concluded.
articles.body:
With the stock market posting a remarkable rebound in the past 24 hours, and the outlook relatively rosy heading into 2027, there's little to tip the wings of investors right now. And yet, whispers of a dreaded recession are coming from figures that Wall Street cannot afford to ignore. Among those sounding the alarm is Bill Ackman, the hedge fund titan who leads Pershing Square. Ackman's concerns lie with the Federal Reserve, and whether it will raise rates at its next meeting in the second week of December.

Ackman wrote on X that financial conditions have already tightened significantly courtesy of the bond market, making borrowing even more expensive for private businesses seeking to invest. Capital expenditure, in AI infrastructure in particular, has been a key driver for the U.S. and global economy for the past year.

"The Fed's 2% inflation ambition is misguided. Geopolitical risk and the required investment in global military spending, deglobalization and tariffs, and the massive AI infrastructure and related energy investment are features of the world that did not exist when the 2% target was set," he said earlier this week (ahead of Jensen Huang's return to chipmaker Nvidia , which prompted a swift turnaround in stock market futures).

"Three percent inflation is a more realistic ambition in the new world," he said.

Ackman's call to end the Fed's 2% inflation target would have far-reaching implications, if implemented. For one, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh has made it clear he wants to give consumers and businesses a break from prices rising comfortably above the 2% benchmark. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' most recent data, inflation is 3.7% annually.

Economists could make a plethora of arguments as to why a 2% target was introduced and should stay in place, but chief among them would also likely be the Fed's credibility. As Warsh learned this year, if markets perceive any weakness in the central bank's commitment to the 2% target, they will raise their inflation expectations in the longer term. This summer, that meant bond prices rose—Ackman's very concern.

And yet, a realist might argue that macroeconomic conditions at present make it practically impossible for the Fed to bring inflation back to 2%—while also being mindful of the other side of its mandate: to maintain employment levels. Apollo's chief economist, Torsten Slok, noted earlier this month that, according to its modeling, the Fed would need to raise the base rate by approximately 275 basis points (from roughly 4% at present to 6.75% by the end of 2027) to bring the consumer price index back to its 2% target.

articles.title: O’Reilly: Saying Huang is innocent ‘just gives Bernie Sanders more power’
articles.summary: Political commentator Bill O’Reilly criticized President Trump’s support of recently reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has been in the midst of a controversy following reports of his relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. “I disagree with the president on the action. But I do believe in due process” O’Reilly said during an appearance on…
articles.body:
Political commentator Bill O’Reilly criticized President Trump’s support of recently reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has been in the midst of a controversy following reports of his relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

“I disagree with the president on the action. But I do believe in due process” O’Reilly said during an appearance on NewsNation’s “On Balance.” “The way to handle this would have been to suspend Huang and then investigate him for a variety of crimes, including harming the nation.”

The tech CEO was reinstated to his position on Monday , a little more than a week after he resigned. A New York Times report in October claimed American authorities discovered a Chinese businesswoman , Alice Huang, illegally smuggled AI chips into China while developing a “close relationship” with Jensen Huang.

Trump said Monday he “convinced” the Nvidia board to reinstate the CEO, saying, “I spoke to them, let me put it that way.”

Trump has previously defended Huang despite the scandals involving his relationships. The president told CNBC that the U.S. did a “thorough investigation” and it showed Huang did “nothing wrong.”

“To say that he, Huang, is innocent, just gives Bernie Sanders more power,” O’Reilly said, adding “the president in defending Huang, on saying that he didn’t do anything wrong, allows the opposition to run wild.”

The Nvidia CEO previously acknowledged that he had been unfaithful to his wife, adding, “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” according to a report from Bloomberg .

Following his reinstatement, Huang said he was “honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution.”

Nvidia’s stocks surged as the CEO returned, with the company closing out Monday at $165.05 per share, a nearly 31.5 percent increase from Friday’s closing bell.

O’Reilly during the NewsNation interview called for Huang’s suspension, saying, “Yes, the stock market would have taken a hit. Yes, temporarily, people would have lost money. I’m willing to accept that for a nation that operates in a fair way.”

articles.title: Support for childhood vaccinations ticks up: Gallup
articles.summary: A greater share of Americans say they believe it is important for parents to vaccinate their children than they did two years ago, according to a new poll released Tuesday. The Gallup survey found that 72 percent of Americans support childhood immunization — up from 69 percent in 2024. Additionally, the new poll found a 7-point…
articles.body:
A greater share of Americans say they believe it is important for parents to vaccinate their children than they did two years ago, according to a new poll released Tuesday.

The Gallup survey found that 72 percent of Americans support childhood immunization — up from 69 percent in 2024. Additionally, the new poll found a 7-point uptick in respondents who said it is “extremely” important for children to be vaccinated.

Forty-seven percent of people in this year’s poll said it was “extremely” important, while 25 percent said it was “very important” for parents to get their kids vaccinated.

These totals are down from the survey’s high in 2001, when 94 percent of respondents said it was important for kids to be vaccinated, including 64 percent who said it was “extremely” important.

The Gallup poll was conducted in October, amid rising measles cases across the country. This year has been the worst year for measles in more than three decades, with the number of infections more than doubling that of last year.

States such as Texas, New Mexico, New York, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin have all reported measles-related deaths. On Monday, the Pennsylvania Department of Health confirmed the ninth measles-associated death in the state and a total of 1,638 cases and 330 hospitalizations tied to the outbreak.

The Pennsylvania health agency said Monday it has administered more than 7,400 MMR vaccinations at pop-up clinics in affected communities.

Last week, the U.S. lost its measles elimination status — a distinction it had held for more than a quarter of a century — along with countries such as Bolivia and Mexico. A country loses its elimination status after experiencing a year of sustained domestic transmission.

Following the news, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said his administration was committed to working with state health agencies to fight the spread of measles.

“We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status,” he wrote in a social media post . “I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.”

The Gallup survey was conducted Oct. 1-19 among a sample of 1,200 U.S. adults with a margin of error of approximately 4 percentage points.

articles.title: Apple tightens Mac security as AI agents seek your files
articles.summary: Apple's macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds new Mac security controls for AI agents, letting you pick specific protected folders instead of granting Full Disk Access.
articles.body: Ever download an app on your Mac and click through the permission requests without giving them much thought? You're certainly not alone. But what if one of those approvals gave an AI assistant access to your private messages, financial documents or even files you thought were protected? That's the concern behind Apple's latest Mac security controls. As AI agents become more capable of performing tasks on your computer, they're also requesting access to more personal information. And once you grant certain permissions, an app could potentially see far more than you intended. Now, Apple is introducing new protections in macOS 27.3 that give you greater control over what these apps can access. The changes arrived in macOS 27.3 beta 2 on Nov. 16, with the broader software release still to come. Here's what Apple is changing and why you may want to check your Mac's privacy settings now. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. MALICIOUS BROWSER EXTENSIONS CAN HIJACK AI ASSISTANTS Why AI agents are raising new Mac security concerns AI assistants have become increasingly useful, especially when you want help getting through a long list of tasks. An AI agent can go further by interacting with apps and taking actions on your behalf. For example, you might ask an AI agent to organize your Downloads folder or find a receipt buried in your email. To complete those tasks, the software may request permission to access information stored on your Mac. That's where things can get uncomfortable. Some apps request a powerful macOS permission called Full Disk Access, which can give them access to nearly everything stored on your computer, including information from other apps. Apple warns that an app with this permission can read or modify sensitive files. It may also be able to delete or export information without asking you again. And the potential exposure goes beyond documents. Another powerful permission, called System & App Protection Override, can allow an app to control your Mac and monitor activity, including keystrokes, when you grant unrestricted access. That's a lot of trust to place in software, especially when an AI agent can take actions without asking you to approve every step. What Apple is changing in macOS 27.3 Apple's upcoming update introduces several changes designed to make powerful permissions easier to understand. It also gives Mac owners more opportunities to limit access before an app starts working. Clearer warnings when apps request powerful permissions Apple is separating its existing Device Control and Data Access permission system into two settings: System & App Protection Override and Accessibility. The change helps clarify when an app is requesting permission to bypass built-in protections. Apple is also introducing more detailed warnings about the information an app could access if you approve its request. Instead of clicking through a vague permission prompt, you'll have more information about what you're allowing. More control over which files an AI agent can access One of the biggest changes involves Full Disk Access. Starting with macOS 27.3, some apps requesting this permission will let you choose specific protected folders instead of granting access to everything. Other apps may continue using the existing approval process, depending on their purpose. For example, an AI tool helping you organize work documents may only need access to one folder. You could grant that limited permission while keeping other protected information off-limits. Apple is also introducing a more consistent process for granting these permissions. You'll select the requesting app from a list rather than navigating different approval methods. AI agents can be required to ask before taking control Another important addition gives you more control over how AI agents interact with other apps. When configuring System & App Protection Override, you can choose which apps an AI tool may control. For each approved app, you can select Ask First or At Any Time. Choosing Ask First means the AI agent must request permission before controlling that app. That extra confirmation may slow down some automated tasks, but it also gives you an opportunity to catch unwanted actions. Apple is adding a transparency indicator that appears when an app controls another app through this permission system. That could make it easier to recognize when software is acting on your behalf. MAC MALWARE CAN HIDE COMMANDS IN YOUR ICLOUD CALENDAR Why Apple is tightening AI agent security now Apple's announcement follows growing scrutiny over how much information AI-powered software can access. In September, a journalist claimed that Meta's Muse AI app had read his private messages without his permission. Meta disputed that account, saying the Messages integration requires explicit permission. Separately, a security vulnerability in OpenAI's ChatGPT Mac app could have allowed attackers to access sensitive information. OpenAI patched the flaw before it was publicly reported. These incidents highlight the security concerns surrounding increasingly capable AI software. Even legitimate applications can create privacy risks when they receive broad access to personal information. Apple's response focuses on making those permissions more visible and giving people greater control over what they approve. Importantly, the changes won't prevent you from installing AI agents or using apps that genuinely need broader permissions. One important catch with Apple's new Mac security controls There's something worth knowing before assuming the update will automatically protect everything on your Mac. Apple says permissions you've already granted will remain in effect after the update. The new approval experience primarily applies when apps request permissions going forward. That means an AI app you installed months ago could still have access to information you previously approved. You'll need to review those permissions yourself if you want to change them. Apple is also allowing developers of certain backup and accessibility applications to request special permissions that preserve their existing functionality. This should help prevent legitimate tools from losing features they need to operate. How to check which apps have access to your Mac You can review your Mac's privacy permissions now, even before macOS 27.3 becomes widely available. Steps may vary slightly depending on your version of macOS. If you find an app with permissions it no longer needs, you can revoke its access. Depending on your macOS version, you may see a toggle or an option to remove the app from the permission list. For macOS 27.3: Select an app and click the Remove (−) button to revoke access. To replace broad access with a more limited permission, remove the app and add it again. When prompted, choose the specific protected folders or apps it needs. Keep in mind that some legitimate applications, including backup software and security tools, require extensive access to function properly. Removing their permissions could prevent certain features from working. AI CHATBOT PRIVACY: WHAT YOUR AI MAY KNOW ABOUT YOU Tips to protect your privacy when using AI agents on a Mac You don't have to stop using AI assistants to protect your information. A few precautions can help you take advantage of these tools while reducing unnecessary exposure. 1. Give AI agents only the access they need When an app requests access to your files, consider whether it needs permission to browse your entire Mac. If the new macOS controls offer a Choose Folder or Choose Apps option, use it to limit the information the software can reach. You can adjust those permissions later if the app needs additional access. 2. Make AI agents ask before controlling other apps If you're using macOS 27.3, look for the Ask First setting when granting an AI agent permission to control another application. This gives you another opportunity to review what the software wants to do. It's especially useful when an AI tool interacts with apps containing sensitive personal information. 3. Download AI software from trusted sources Be careful when installing new AI agents, particularly from unfamiliar websites. We've previously reported how AI-related scams target Mac owners through convincing fake download pages. Stick with official developer websites or the Mac App Store whenever possible. Keep your installed apps updated to receive security fixes. 4. Use strong antivirus software Your Mac includes built-in malware protection, but reputable antivirus software can add another layer of security. It can help detect malicious downloads and other threats, including malware disguised as legitimate AI tools. However, antivirus software can't reliably prevent an app from accessing information you've already given it permission to use. That's why reviewing your Mac's privacy settings remains important. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. 5. Review the privacy policy before sharing sensitive information Even when an app has limited access to your files, you should understand how it handles information you choose to share. Check whether the developer stores your data or sends it to cloud servers. Apple's permission controls can restrict access to protected information on your Mac, but they don't replace an app's privacy policy. 6. Revisit permissions as your needs change An AI tool may have needed access to a particular folder when you first installed it. That doesn't mean it needs the same permission indefinitely. Periodically check Privacy & Security and remove access that no longer serves a purpose. This is particularly important for AI apps you rarely use. 7. Back up important files before letting AI agents make changes If you're allowing an AI agent to organize or modify files, make sure you have a recent backup. An automated task could accidentally delete something important or change a document you wanted to keep. Apple's built-in Time Machine can automatically back up your Mac and help you recover files if something goes wrong. For step-by-step instructions, check out our guide on how to back up your computer. Kurt's key takeaways I'm glad Apple is taking a closer look at how much access AI agents can have on our computers. These tools are becoming more capable, and I can see why people would want an assistant that handles repetitive work. But giving an app permission to see everything on your Mac seems like a steep price to pay for convenience. I particularly like the option to make an AI agent ask before controlling another app. That's a level of oversight I would want, especially when personal information is involved. My biggest concern is that previously granted permissions will remain active. Apple can introduce better warnings, but those warnings won't change the decisions you've already made. I'd encourage Mac owners to spend a few minutes reviewing their settings rather than waiting for the next update. Would you trust an AI assistant with unrestricted access to your Mac if it could save you hours of work, or does the thought of software reading your private information cross a line? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. Sign up for my FREE CyberGuy Newsletter CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Copyright 2026 CyberGuy.com. All rights reserved.

articles.title: Top House Democrat calls for public hearing with Jensen Huang
articles.summary: A ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee on Tuesday called for a public hearing from recently reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has been facing mounting scrutiny over reports of a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. “The American People deserve to hear publicly from Mr. Huang about how potentially billions of dollars’…
articles.body:
A ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee on Tuesday called for a public hearing from recently reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has been facing mounting scrutiny over reports of a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

“The American People deserve to hear publicly from Mr. Huang about how potentially billions of dollars’ worth of our most advanced technology wound up in the hands of our greatest competitor, and what role this administration played,” Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.) wrote in a statement, shared by the House committee on the social platform X .

Huang was reinstated to his position on Monday , a little more than a week after he resigned. A New York Times report in October claimed American authorities discovered a Chinese businesswoman , Alice Huang, illegally smuggled AI chips into China while developing a “close relationship” with the Nvidia CEO.

President Trump said Monday he “convinced” the Nvidia board to reinstate Jensen Huang, saying, “I spoke to them, let me put it that way.”

He has previously defended Huang despite the scandals involving his extramarital affairs. The president told CNBC that the U.S. did a “thorough investigation” and it showed Huang did “nothing wrong.”

“President Trump’s intervention to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO raises even more concerning questions about the administration’s own role, questions the American people deserve to hear answered in public,” Meeks wrote in his statement.

Following Huang’s return, Nvidia’s stocks surged , with the company closing out Monday at $165.05 per share, a nearly 31.5 percent increase from Friday’s closing bell.

House Republicans said Huang and Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter have “confirmed they will appear for their transcribed interviews on December 1 and December 2.”

“The NVIDIA board’s brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast (R-Fla.), House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party Chair John Moolenaar (R-Mich.) and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) wrote in a joint statement.

Nvidia’s board previously announced it would initiate an independent investigation into the matter and hired former acting U.S. Attorney Joon H. Kim and his firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, to conduct the investigation. The company plans to continue the probe after the Nvidia chief’s reinstatement.

Huang is also set to testify before the Senate Banking Committee in December.

articles.title: Romney on AI, Huang scandal: ‘Smells of profit, corruption and perhaps worse’
articles.summary: Former Sen. Mitt Romney (R-Utah) on Tuesday criticized the federal government’s handling of artificial intelligence and export regulation. “Let me get this straight: we rushed AI along without regulating safeguards in order to stay ahead of China and at the same time, we sold China the very chips they’d need to get ahead of us.…
articles.body:
Former Sen. Mitt Romney (R-Utah) on Tuesday criticized the federal government’s handling of artificial intelligence and export regulation.

“Let me get this straight: we rushed AI along without regulating safeguards in order to stay ahead of China and at the same time, we sold China the very chips they’d need to get ahead of us. Smells of profit, corruption and perhaps worse,” the 2012 GOP nominee for president said in a post on the social platform X on Tuesday morning.

Romney’s comments come in the wake of Jensen Huang, an ally of President Trump, being reinstated as the CEO of Nvidia. Huang came back to the role a little more than a week after he stepped down amid an affair scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s board chair, said in a statement Monday.

“We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company,” he continued.

Earlier this month , Huang resigned as Nvidia’s president and CEO following reports he had an extramarital affair with a former senior executive at Megaspeed who was alleged to have been in contact with a Chinese spy agency.

Megaspeed bought billions of dollars’ worth of advanced chips from Nvidia, with American officials suspecting that it may have evaded export controls.

On Monday, the Commerce Department took action to place Megaspeed on its trade entity blacklist, per federal records. The move was published in the Federal Register on Monday, and it came amid increasing pressure on the Commerce Department to tighten its chip export controls in the wake of reports that Megaspeed was accused of helping smuggle Nvidia’s chips to China.

The Hill has reached out to Nvidia for comment.

articles.title: UK warns AI-driven cyberattacks are exposing years of weak security | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The British cyber agency says that "building strong foundations has never mattered more" as AI hacking tools rely on exploiting simple security flaws.
articles.body:
The U.K. government’s cybersecurity unit says it has seen a “marked rise” in AI-driven cyberattacks in recent months, as hackers increasingly rely on autonomous hacking tools to identify and exploit simple weaknesses to break into systems and networks.

The U.K. National Cybersecurity Center (NCSC) said it has seen several cyber incidents since September involving autonomous hacking tools, such as penetration testing tools used by defenders to stress-test their cybersecurity defenses. These incidents have caused intrusions at organizations and resulted in downtime, the unit said in a blog post .

The NCSC says that while none of the vulnerabilities being exploited are new, the speed at which these AI tools are able to carry out simple hacks has changed.

The rise in AI-related cyberattacks coincides with the broader release earlier this year of open source autonomous penetration testing tools like Artex and Cairn, among others, which anyone can download and use at no cost. The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation recently warned that malicious hackers are using AI penetration testing tools to carry out cyberattacks at unprecedented speeds.

While cyberattacks and intrusions are on the rise, the message from London is that many of these attacks are preventable with basic cybersecurity defenses and best practices.

“Notably, the issues being exploited currently are not novel memory corruption vulnerabilities (or even known but unpatched vulnerabilities), but unmitigated weaknesses that are often the result of years of technical debt that organisations have accumulated,” the NCSC wrote.

The unit said that agentic hacking tools often look for exposed or internet-facing systems, then quickly run through lists of weak or easy-to-guess passwords or abuse API endpoints often used by developers to access data.

The NCSC said that AI “does not make established cyber security controls obsolete,” but rather that “building strong foundations has never mattered more.”

The unit added that AI has made it easier to find vulnerabilities and faster to exploit them, warning that weaknesses that have gone unnoticed for years can now be found in minutes.

articles.title: Iowa governor backs Army’s lead detonation even as safety questions remain
articles.summary: Outgoing Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds (R) said Tuesday she supports the Army’s planned detonation of nearly five tons of lead-containing munitions in her state, which is set for Wednesday morning despite an outcry from environmental groups and residents. Planned at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, the detonation will move forward after a federal appeals…
articles.body:
Outgoing Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds (R) said Tuesday she supports the Army’s planned detonation of nearly five tons of lead-containing munitions in her state, which is set for Wednesday morning despite an outcry from environmental groups and residents.

Planned at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, the detonation will move forward after a federal appeals court on Monday declined to halt it , even as environmental groups argued that the U.S. government did not give the public enough notice of the plan.

The groups say the event will expose thousands of families, livestock and crops in surrounding communities to elevated levels of toxic dust.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

But Reynolds said she takes seriously the Army’s warning that a planned detonation is necessary over what the service has claimed could be an uncontrolled explosion.

“I believe, based on the information I’ve been given, that the danger is immediate, and I trust the Army will do everything in its power to protect the people who could be affected,” Reynolds said in a statement posted to social platform X.

She added that she spoke with several Cabinet members and Army leadership in recent days, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and acting Army Secretary Adam Telle, and has asked the military branch for more information to help her state prepare for before and after the blast. Reynolds said she has “been assured that it will be provided.”

Iowa last week opened its State Emergency Operations Center to coordinate with federal officials “to keep Iowans safe and informed,” she noted.

“As governor, the safety of Iowans near the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is my top priority,” Reynolds said.

There has been significant public confusion over the forthcoming detonation meant to destroy nearly 10,000 pounds of degraded lead azide at the ammunition plant.

The Army on Nov. 15 issued a public advisory stating that in five days, it planned to detonate the material, resulting in a massive plume with lead-containing particles in the air — even as it insisted it was the safest way to eliminate what it described as an “explosive safety hazard.”

That came after it was revealed the service at least since March had known about the degraded lead azide and even canceled a contract to have it chemically disposed of.

The Army’s detonation plans and the short notice it provided stirred public outrage, with environmental organizations suing over the Environmental Protection Agency’s emergency permit for the activity. The detonation was then moved first to Monday and later to Wednesday.

President Trump on Monday stepped in and placed the ultimate decision on whether to move forward on both the courts and incoming Gov. Rob Sand (D), a determination that Sand quickly punted back .

Sand said the federal government should make the call on the detonation but added: “Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation, and learn why the administration believes this is the best path forward.”

Iowa Sen. Joni Ernst (R), meanwhile, said the Army began discussing disposal with some communities months ago, but “critical details, including the potential lead plume and how far it could reach, were not part of those initial conversations.”

In a statement released Tuesday, she said many neighboring communities weren’t included in talks at all and only learned of the potential plume last week.

“Iowans deserved that information much sooner,” Ernst said.

“At a time when trust in our institutions is already low, the military owes the people it serves more transparency, not less. These materials should never have been allowed to get to this point, and Iowans are right to be frustrated,” she noted.

Ernst added that she understands the risks of further delay after meeting with Army leaders and federal officials, will press them for answers, and supports efforts to reduce the public’s exposure to lead.

Lead is a toxic metal that can be particularly harmful to babies and children, and exposure can cause brain damage, nervous system damage, learning problems, behavioral issues and a lower IQ.

In a press conference Tuesday, Army Col. Aaron Teller, an explosives specialist, said the service will try to limit the amount of lead released into the air by covering the lead azide in two stories’ worth of sand, surrounding it with water tanks and pouring two feet of foam concentrate on top.

Officials sidestepped a question on whether all such mitigation measures were already in place when the explosion was originally to take place on Friday.

The last such major disposal of lead azide was in 1977, when approximately 7,000 pounds of the substance was detonated in open air in Colorado with zero mitigation measures in place.

Teller said in that instance, 25 percent of the lead particles went into the atmosphere, “so we believe we can significantly reduce that last 25 percent with the mitigation strategy that we’ve emplaced.”

articles.title: TSA expects to screen nearly 18M air travelers over Thanksgiving week
articles.summary: The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) announced it was expecting to screen nearly 18 million travelers over the Thanksgiving week following a nationwide ground stop earlier this month that disrupted millions of travelers. “TSA is prepared to handle the increased passenger volumes expected during the Thanksgiving holiday travel period while maintaining our focus on security,” TSA…
articles.body:
The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) announced it was expecting to screen nearly 18 million travelers over the Thanksgiving week following a nationwide ground stop earlier this month that disrupted millions of travelers.

“TSA is prepared to handle the increased passenger volumes expected during the Thanksgiving holiday travel period while maintaining our focus on security,” TSA Administrator David Cummins said in a statement.

The TSA is predicting to screen approximately 17.6 million air travelers nationwide between Nov. 24 and Nov. 30. The busiest day of the Thanksgiving holiday period is anticipated on Nov. 29, with 3 million passengers at U.S. airports traveling.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) similarly projected the busiest holiday skies in 16 years, with more than 417,000 forecast flights over a nine-day holiday period. Tuesday is scheduled to be the busiest travel day, with 52,345 flights forecast to take off.

After the holidays, 44,265 flights are planned on Saturday, and 50,314 are slated for Sunday, according to the FAA.

The agencies both warned that forecast weather could disrupt travel. On Tuesday, a low layer of overcast could affect flights along the West Coast, while thunderstorms near Florida and the Gulf Coast are expected to impact flights on Wednesday.

Travel through the country’s busiest airport in Atlanta, Ga., is expected to be disrupted by rain in parts of the Southeast before moving into the mid-Atlantic.

Forecasters are also predicting a storm system could bring heavy rain, strong winds and potential flooding, which will likely impact Thanksgiving travel for many in the Northeast.

Thanksgiving-week travel comes as the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13, which interrupted travel for millions of travelers. The rare protocol was in place for nearly four hours . The agency has cited a router in Arkansas and a radar site in Texas as the two likely causes of the outage.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wrote in a statement Tuesday that his department has already “taken unprecedented action to limit flight delays and cancellations” by “using a successful new platform to predict and address congestion in the airspace.”

“The American people can rest assured we will be on the clock 24/7 to get families to their destinations safely and on time,” Duffy said.

At the time of the outage, he called for additional congressional funding to modernize the FAA’s air traffic control systems.

articles.title: Now Firefox can select which sites use its VPN, and clear your browsing history with one click
articles.summary: Firefox’s “Manage VPN rules” setting chooses which websites open with its built-in VPN automatically turned on.
articles.body: Mozilla released Firefox 161 on Tuesday with a new setting you can use to choose which pages automatically open with the browser’s VPN active. Using the “Manage VPN rules” option in Firefox’s VPN panel, you can set it to “always on” or “always off” for specific sites, so you don’t have to toggle it manually every time you visit certain pages. Starting Tuesday, Mozilla is also rolling out a “Fire” button in standard Firefox windows that lets you quickly clear your browsing data directly from the toolbar. You can choose which data it deletes, including browsing history, downloads history, cookie data, site data, temporary files, saved form info, and website permissions and preferences. If you set the button to delete all of that data, clicking it will sign you out of everything and open a fresh Firefox window. Tuesday’s Firefox update also adds an option for creating a keyboard shortcut for copying your current tab’s URL, and brings its “read aloud” option in Reader Mode to the Android version of Firefox. Alongside the update, Mozilla says Firefox is also now available directly through the Play Store on cars with Google built-in.

articles.title: Weather threatens Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. Has it ever been canceled?
articles.summary: Macy’s has never outright canceled a Thanksgiving Day Parade on account of weather. But several have been canceled for another reason.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Wind and heavy rains could dampen the mood at the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City on Thursday, as a powerful nor’easter is expected to move across the region just in time for the festivities.

The winds, in particular, may also pose a problem for those hoping to see the parade’s 100 scheduled balloons, as New York regulations mandate they be grounded if sustained winds or gusts exceed the safety thresholds.

The last time the parade’s balloons were grounded was in 1971, when wind and rain reportedly prevented many of the familiar floating figures from being flown. Other parade elements, like floats and performances, continued mostly as planned.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“Donald Duck couldn’t come. Neither could Snoopy. Or Linus the Lionhearted. Or even Smokey the Bear,” The New York Times wrote of the festivities that year. “It was too windy, their managers explained.”

In a statement shared with Nexstar, a representative for Macy’s said event planners are “closely monitoring the weather forecast with our City and agency partners, and as always, the safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority.”

A decision about the balloons has yet to be made, the spokesperson added.

Macy’s, meanwhile, has never outright canceled a Thanksgiving Day Parade on account of weather. But they were indeed canceled between 1942–1944 during World War II.

In an announcement published on Thanksgiving during that WWII hiatus, Macy’s explained (via a poem, and also a notice written from the perspective of the balloons ) that the materials that would have otherwise gone into staging the event — e.g., helium, rubber, auto parts, gasoline — were being conserved for the war effort.

“We’d like to act as barrage balloons, too, and hang around New York or London. But it’s up to the armed forces. What they say goes,” the balloons “wrote” in a portion of the notice. “And whatever assignment we draw, we’ll swell with pride (helium or no helium) knowing that we’re going to help deflate Hitler and his chums.”

As of Tuesday, the nor’easter forecasted for Thursday is expected to bring rain and sustained winds, with wind gusts “as high as 55 mph,” according to a Tuesday forecast from the National Weather Service.

“Decisions regarding balloon flight will be made on Parade morning based on weather conditions and established safety protocols,” the Macy’s representative said.

articles.title: GLP-1s could prevent millions of deaths, free up farmland: Study
articles.summary: The research is the latest in surprising findings suggesting that the drugs originally meant to treat diabetes have wider-ranging impacts.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — A new study suggests widespread use of weight loss medications such as Ozempic and Mounjaro could prevent millions of global deaths and free up farmland area larger than that of Italy by 2050.

“With widespread use of these medicines among adults living with obesity, we estimate that reduced calorie intake could prevent up to 6.6 million deaths each year by 2050, while freeing up as much as 32 million hectares of agricultural land — an area slightly larger than Italy — for other uses,” according to the study’s authors .

The research was conducted by scientists from Aberdeen, the University of Edinburgh and Scotland’s Rural College and published in the journal “Nature Communications.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

It is the latest in a series of surprising findings suggesting that drugs originally meant to treat diabetes have wider-ranging impacts .

Last year, a separate study analyzing 92,000 people found semaglutides, found in GLP-1 drugs, were linked to a 33 percent lower risk of dementia , among other health benefits.

An economic study found that GLP-1 medications , including Ozempic and Wegovy, led to employees taking 17 percent less long-term sick time.

The study, published by the National Bureau of Economic Research, defined “long-term” as absences of more than 30 days related to illness and used Danish data to examine the connection between the drugs and absences.

Ongoing research suggests the medications could have other positive impacts, including reduced risks of cardiovascular disease and some cancers .

NewsNation’s Steph Whiteside and Patrick Djordjevic contributed to this report.

articles.title: Reporters grill Blanche over handling of Huang affair, Nvidia chip exports
articles.summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche pushed back on numerous questions Tuesday about the government’s probes into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s alleged affair with a suspected Chinese spy and potential export control violations. During a press conference about cyber crimes, Blanche fielded questions about President Trump’s remarks a day earlier, when he said Jensen Huang was “exonerated”…
articles.body:
Attorney General Todd Blanche pushed back on numerous questions Tuesday about the government’s probes into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s alleged affair with a suspected Chinese spy and potential export control violations .

During a press conference about cyber crimes, Blanche fielded questions about President Trump’s remarks a day earlier, when he said Jensen Huang was “exonerated” following unspecified investigations into the executive and whether Nvidia chips were diverted to China.

When asked by a reporter whether the Department of Justice (DOJ) investigated Jensen Huang, Blanche said, “What the president said is that he talked to a lot of people going into the decision that he made to encourage the board to reinstate him.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“And so, I’m not going to get into communications I have with the president about it,” Blanche continued. “What he was saying was true, right? What he was saying is exactly right, which is that, to the extent that the Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes or something like this, that’s something that I would have certainly told the president had it been true.”

A reporter followed up, asking again whether Jensen Huang had been investigated.

“What does that mean? Had Huang been investigated? For what?” Blanche responded. “I don’t understand the question … even the reporting from the various leaks or sources or whatever that was out there, didn’t suggest Huang himself was under some sort of investigation. At least not that I saw.”

The DOJ and Commerce Department confirmed they were investigating Megaspeed , the company at the center of Nvidia’s national security scandal but did not detail specific probes into Jensen Huang or the company.

Trump alluded to government investigations in an interview with CNBC on Monday, but he did not specify the agencies or subjects involved.

When asked what Blanche told him about potential criminal liability for Jensen Huang, Trump told CNBC, “Well they did a study, they did a pretty good investigation, and they felt that he, himself, was exonerated … I don’t know what word to use.”

Trump also said Monday on Truth Social that the government has “no reason to believe” Jensen Huang is a national security risk and “does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.”

The president was quick to take credit for his role in the Nvidia board’s change of heart on Jensen Huang, who resigned less than two weeks earlier due to a scandal over an alleged affair with Alice Huang, a former executive of the Singaporean data center firm Megaspeed whom U.S. intelligence officials suspected was gathering intel for China.

Nvidia’s board of directors unanimously voted to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO and president, just days after telling investors it was not considering his return.

Meanwhile, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have vowed investigations into Jensen Huang and Nvidia over potential national security risks and chip export violations.

Asked on Tuesday about export control investigations, Blanche told a reporter, “I don’t know what you’re talking about. We have hundreds, if not more, export investigations going at any time” at the DOJ.

On Nov. 12, Blanche affirmed the DOJ has a role in investigating potential violations of chip export laws — many of which are “ongoing” — but he declined to comment on any particular probe.

The attorney general also declined to share any findings from the intelligence community about Alice Huang, stating it “is not something that we should be sharing with the media.”

“Nvidia is a good corporate citizen,” Blanche said. “That’s not … that shouldn’t be groundbreaking.”
