articles.title: What United Airlines banning AI agents from booking flights means for your travel plans
articles.summary: United Airlines is blocking unauthorized AI travel agents from its booking systems, warning that automated purchases could put MileagePlus miles at risk.
articles.body: Wouldn't it be nice to tell an AI assistant to find the cheapest flight to your destination and book your favorite seat while you do something else? That kind of convenience is getting closer. But United Airlines wants to make sure an unauthorized AI assistant never gets that far. The airline is restricting third-party AI agents from accessing its booking systems without permission. United says these tools could expose sensitive customer information and make purchases travelers never intended to authorize. The concern also extends to MileagePlus accounts, where an automated mistake could put valuable airline miles at risk. The decision comes as AI assistants become increasingly capable of taking action on our behalf. While that sounds convenient, United is raising questions about how much control we should give software over our travel plans. Here's where United draws the line and what you need to know before letting AI handle your next flight booking. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. FORMER ANTHROPIC SECURITY LEADER WARNS AI AGENTS ARE BECOMING TOO AUTONOMOUS FOR HUMANS TO KEEP THEM IN CHECK Why United Airlines is blocking AI agents On Nov. 11, United Airlines published an official news release titled United Restricts Access for Third-Party AI Agents. The airline explained that protecting customer information and account security prompted the restrictions. According to United, sharing account credentials with personal AI assistants can expose sensitive information. The airline also warned that automated actions might lead to unwanted purchases or changes to existing reservations. Then there's the issue of frequent flyer miles. United specifically mentioned the possibility that an AI assistant could use MileagePlus miles without the traveler intending that redemption. To address those concerns, United is restricting unauthorized personal AI agents from accessing its digital platforms. The rules also reach travel agencies and booking services that might use automated AI tools to access United's systems. United says it is updating its policies to support these restrictions. The airline also plans to continue evaluating how personal AI assistants interact with its services. What exactly is an AI travel agent? You may already use AI to research vacation destinations or figure out which airport is closest to your hotel. An AI travel agent takes that technology further by performing tasks for you. For example, you could ask an AI assistant to find a flight under $400 that arrives before dinner. Instead of simply recommending flights, an AI agent might search booking systems and attempt to complete the reservation. Some agents can also interact with websites using a browser. That means they may be able to enter personal information and complete steps that normally require you to click through a booking process. The convenience is easy to understand. However, granting an AI assistant access to your airline account can also give it the ability to make changes you never intended. For more on what these assistants can do, see our article on eight seriously annoying tasks you can hand off to an AI agent. United says AI agents could create airline safety problems United's concerns go beyond account security. The airline also warns that automated AI activity could potentially violate Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and Department of Transportation (DOT) regulations. Consider what happens when you check in for a flight. Airlines require travelers to acknowledge important safety information, including whether their bags contain prohibited hazardous materials. United specifically points to the requirement for a person to confirm that baggage contains no banned substances, such as explosives. An AI assistant handling check-in could potentially bypass that acknowledgment. After all, how would an AI assistant know what you actually packed in your suitcase? United has identified this as a potential regulatory concern. The airline has not established that every AI-assisted check-in violates federal law. Could United cancel a flight booked by an AI agent? This may be the biggest concern for travelers experimenting with automated booking tools. United revised its Contract of Carriage on Nov. 11. The updated rules prohibit AI agents from making or modifying tickets and purchasing airline products or services. The contract also identifies reservations made or changed through AI agents as subject to cancellation without advance notice. The definition of an AI agent includes automated tools even when a traveler supervises or approves their actions. However, there is an important exception for existing reservations. United says bookings made by AI agents before Nov. 11, will not be canceled under the new restriction. The airline recommends reviewing those reservations to confirm that they were properly booked and ticketed. If you previously used an AI assistant to arrange United travel, open the United app or website and verify your itinerary. Check that your ticket was actually issued rather than assuming a booking confirmation means everything is complete. You can review the airline's published rules in its Contract of Carriage at united.com/en/us/fly/contract-of-carriage.html. MALICIOUS BROWSER EXTENSIONS CAN HIJACK AI ASSISTANTS Can you still use AI to plan a United Airlines trip? Yes, although United has established limits on how outside AI tools can interact with its systems. You can still ask an AI chatbot for general travel advice or help creating an itinerary. United's guidance allows AI-assisted research and trip planning as long as the tool does not access United's website or app. However, an unauthorized AI agent cannot search United's website or app on your behalf. The restriction also covers automated purchasing and reservation management. That means an AI-powered browser feature that automatically searches United's website could fall under the restriction, even if it never buys a ticket. United says assistive technology for travelers with disabilities remains unaffected. Traditional travel booking services can also continue operating through permitted channels. The restriction specifically addresses unauthorized AI agents, including those used by travel agencies. According to United's published guidance, the airline does not currently work with any third-party AI agents under this policy. Southwest Airlines is taking a different approach to AI While United is putting restrictions in place, Southwest Airlines is exploring a different approach. On Oct. 6, Southwest announced a ChatGPT integration. The feature allows you to discover destinations and shop for Southwest flights directly through ChatGPT. However, Southwest's integration still directs you to the airline's website to complete purchases. The company describes the arrangement as an early step toward broader AI-powered booking capabilities. That approach gives Southwest a way to use AI for flight discovery while maintaining control over the final transaction. United is taking a more restrictive position on outside AI assistants. The airline says it will continue evaluating the technology as it develops. How to protect your United Airlines bookings and miles If you normally book flights through United's website or app, you can continue doing so. You can also use permitted travel booking services. However, if you've started experimenting with AI assistants that make purchases or manage accounts on your behalf, United's restrictions deserve your attention. An AI agent with access to your airline account could potentially reach sensitive travel information. Depending on its permissions, it might also make purchases you never intended to authorize. Here are a few ways to protect yourself. 1) Keep your airline account credentials private Avoid giving third-party AI assistants your MileagePlus password or other sensitive login information. If you've already shared your credentials with an AI agent, United recommends changing your password immediately. You should also remove any saved login details from the AI service. Consider using a password manager to create and securely store a strong, unique password for your airline account. This can help protect your account if a password you use elsewhere gets exposed in a data breach. 2) Use strong antivirus software Strong antivirus software can help protect your devices from malware and malicious links designed to steal login credentials. This is especially important if you use travel booking websites or receive airline confirmation emails. While antivirus protection won't stop an AI assistant from making an unauthorized reservation, it can help prevent cybercriminals from gaining access to your MileagePlus account. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. 3) Book United flights through permitted channels Use United's official website or app, or a booking provider operating under United's rules. United currently does not work with third-party AI agents under this policy. Even if an AI assistant offers to complete a reservation with your approval, that does not necessarily make the transaction permissible. UNITED AIRLINES SAYS TECHNOLOGY ISSUE RESOLVED AFTER ‘WIDESPREAD SYSTEM OUTAGE’ 4) Check your airline miles regularly Review your MileagePlus balance for unexpected activity. If you notice a redemption or purchase you don't recognize, secure your account immediately. Contact United through its official website or app to report the activity and request assistance. 5) Verify reservations before heading to the airport Check your booking confirmation and make sure United has issued your ticket. If an AI assistant arranged your travel before Nov. 11, verify the reservation directly with the airline. United says those earlier bookings will not be canceled under the new restriction. 6) Keep control of purchases and account changes AI can still help you plan a trip using general information without accessing United's systems. However, complete your flight purchases and reservation changes yourself through permitted channels. That way, you can review what you're buying without risking a prohibited AI-agent transaction. Kurt's key takeaways I can see why United is concerned. I've spent enough time searching for flights to appreciate the idea of handing that job over to AI. Let the assistant find me a great fare and save me the hassle of comparing a dozen options. I'm all for that. But the moment it starts making purchases or accessing my airline miles, I want to know exactly what it's doing. I recently spoke with travel expert Katy Nastro, who discovered that someone had stolen 50,000 miles from her American Airlines account. Her experience had nothing to do with AI agents, but it reminded me how much value we keep in these loyalty programs. I certainly wouldn't want an automated mistake putting those rewards at risk. At the same time, I do wonder whether security is the only concern driving United's decision. Airlines have spent years building direct relationships with travelers. AI agents could change how we compare fares and choose which airline gets our business. I would hate to see useful technology held back simply because it gives you more control over the shopping process. United says it will keep evaluating these tools, and I hope that eventually leads to a secure way to book flights using AI. Until then, I'm happy to let AI help find my next trip. I'll take care of the booking myself. Would you trust an AI assistant to book your next flight and access your frequent flyer miles? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. articles.title: GOP senator suggests ‘babysitter’ for Huang to protect US
articles.summary: Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) called for increased export controls following Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia’s CEO, saying Tuesday the tech mogul may pose a “security risk” due to his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. “We’re going to have to put stronger guardrails. We might even have to put a babysitter on Jensen Huang, for…
articles.body:
Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) called for increased export controls following Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia’s CEO, saying Tuesday the tech mogul may pose a “security risk” due to his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

“We’re going to have to put stronger guardrails. We might even have to put a babysitter on Jensen Huang, for crying out loud,” Cramer said during an interview with CNBC.

“If he’s so indispensable that he can’t leave the plant floor, then somebody should probably be right next to him on both sides,” he continued. “Just to make sure that he doesn’t do something that’s going to risk the United States.”

Huang, who also co-founded Nvidia, was reinstated Monday — a little more than a week after he resigned amid the scandal. A late-October New York Times report alleged U.S. authorities discovered a Chinese businessperson , former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, illegally smuggled advanced AI chips into China while developing a “close relationship” with the CEO.

Cramer was among a collection of lawmakers who voiced their support for the Nvidia chief’s resignation earlier this month. Ahead of Jensen Huang’s departure, the North Dakota senator said, “I can’t believe we are even considering him not resigning.”

President Trump said Monday he “convinced” the Nvidia board to reinstate its ousted chief, adding, “I spoke to them, let me put it that way.”

The president previously defended Jensen Huang despite the scandals involving his extramarital affairs and alleged chip sales to China. Trump told CNBC the U.S. did a “thorough investigation” into the reports, and it showed the CEO did “nothing wrong.”

“I can accept what the president has done. I’ll accept that the board now bears all the risk … the reputational risk, as well as the security risk,” Cramer said during his CNBC interview. “They now own that.”

Nvidia’s board previously announced it would initiate an independent investigation into the allegations and hired former acting U.S. District Attorney Joon H. Kim — as well as his firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz — to conduct the investigation. The AI chipmaker plans to continue the probe into Jensen Huang despite his reinstatement.

House Republicans said Jensen Huang and Nvidia’s general counsel , Tim Teter, have “confirmed they will appear for their transcribed interviews on December 1 and December 2.”

The Nvidia chief is also set to testify before the Senate Banking Committee , of which Cramer is a member, in December.

articles.title: Microsoft declares 'Code Red' after historic service outage
articles.summary: Microsoft declared a "Code Red" after a historic 24-hour outage hit most of its 420 to 450 million users that wa blamed on a Windows scalability defect.
articles.body: Tech giant Microsoft declared a "Code Red" alert recently, signaling an urgent effort to address the historic 24-hour outage that downed its core products between Nov. 12-13. The outage, which brought down the majority of Microsoft's core products, "affected most" of Microsoft's users, according to the company's post-incident report. The company's total user base is between 420 million and 450 million people, according to financial disclosures. "Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team," M365 Core President Jason Henderson said in an email to employees Friday obtained by Reuters. DAVID MARCUS: WHAT BIG TECH’S WEEKEND FROM HELL MEANS FOR THE FUTURE OF DATA CENTERS The incident also marked the most customer-impacting event in Microsoft's history, Henderson told employees. Microsoft blamed the outage on a previously undetected scalability defect within the Windows operating system. SWIFT ASSURANCES FROM OFFICIALS AFTER WAVE OF NATIONWIDE OUTAGES RAISES QUESTIONS, EXPERT SAYS "Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday," Henderson wrote. Microsoft employees exchanged over 11,000 messages during the crisis in an effort to diagnose the issue, Microsoft Corporate Vice President Amanda Silver told employees in a memo Monday. DHS CHIEF TELLS AMERICANS TO 'BREATHE' AMID TECH OUTAGES, INSISTS HOMELAND IS 'SECURE' Silver also detailed the nature of the "Code Red" rapid response, explaining that the mobilization would involve five work streams focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning and faster recovery mechanisms. She added that, in the event of a future situation of a similar nature, the company is working on a target to be able to restore service to users within one hour. The company will also work on deploying AI agents to help with quicker diagnosis in the future. LAWMAKERS WARN AMERICANS OF VULNERABLE SYSTEMS AMID STREAK OF OUTAGES: 'SOMETHING IS GOING ON' An estimate from the Anderson Economic Group approximated that the outage cost the global economy roughly $7 billion in lost productivity value. Henderson, in another memo, told employees that urgent patches to Microsoft's flagship M365 suite took too long to deploy. "In a separate recent incident, an urgent production fix took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. For our most urgent security issues, we need to get from detection to safe worldwide deployment in an hour. Needless to say, we aren't here yet," he wrote. articles.title: The clock is running out for America’s most contentious spying law
articles.summary: Warrantless wiretapping proponents are rushing to beat the looming blue wave.
articles.body: Weeks before the end of the legislative session, some members of Congress are scrambling to reauthorize a controversial warrantless wiretapping authority, possibly by attaching it to a must-pass military spending bill. Sen. Mike Rounds (R-SD) told Politico that Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) could be attached to the National Defense Authorization Act. It’s the latest in a grueling fight over a major spying rule that hasn’t technically lapsed. “We don’t have two weeks to work just on FISA,” said Rounds, a member of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence. “But if it’s amended onto the NDAA then you can move it forward and get that done in time.” FISA allows for the warrantless surveillance of certain foreigners’ communications, ostensibly on national security grounds. In part because of FISA’s broad scope, Congress revisits it every few years, both to reauthorize the authority and to reform it. The last effort to do both failed. Despite pressure from President Donald Trump, Congress failed to reauthorize FISA over the summer, in part because leadership wouldn’t allow any amendments — particularly attempts to limit its sweeping scope — to be debated or introduced. (Trump didn’t help matters when he made Bill Pulte the acting director of national intelligence. Pulte, who reportedly bragged about purging one-third of the DNI staff, is now the director of federal housing.) But the surveillance authority didn’t actually lapse because the FISA court rectified surveillance under Section 702 back in March, meaning the surveillance state can keep chugging along as is for another four months. So why the urgency? If you haven’t heard, there’s about to be a new Congress in town — one that is even less likely to give Trump seemingly unlimited spying powers without some semblance of reform. Support for — and opposition to — FISA isn’t a clear-cut partisan issue. Last time around, a bipartisan coalition led by House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) and Rep. Jim Himes (D-CT), the ranking member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, led the campaign for a “clean” reauthorization of FISA. Their efforts were defeated largely because of holdouts from the Freedom Caucus, whose privacy concerns echoed those of liberal lawmakers. FISA’s critics wanted reform, not abolition. Their goal was to make it harder for intelligence agencies to use the statute, which is intended for foreign targets, to access Americans’ communications. “It was remarkable watching two dozen House Republicans stand up to the establishment, stand up to Mike Johnson, and fight to reform FISA,” said Michael Baick, an organizer with the OpenAI boycott campaign QuitGPT, which has been advocating for FISA reform to stop AI surveillance. “This has always been a bipartisan issue where Americans of all stripes can agree, and trying to make deals with the establishment to maintain the status quo, while the ground is shifting, is just short-sighted and missing what this moment really is.” Johnson and Himes were adamantly opposed to any reining in of Section 702, stressing the need for a so-called “clean reauthorization.” Both claimed there had already been reforms. “It ain’t the same FISA,” Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH) declared in April. But the changes reformers most wanted were missing. Among them were a warrant requirement and an end to what critics say are major loopholes. Under Section 702, intelligence agencies can pull the communications of non-US persons not in the United States — that is, foreign nationals outside the country. But federal agencies like the FBI and NSA can buy Americans’ data from private brokers, a practice FBI director Kash Patel admits is ongoing. And intelligence agencies can use Section 702 to obtain the communications of non-US persons who are communicating with Americans — a workaround known as the “backdoor search loophole.” “I think it’s a Hail Mary by surveillance hawks to try to ram through what they wanted to do the entire time,” Don Bell, senior policy counsel at the Constitution Project of the Project on Government Oversight, told The Verge. “This is something everyone knew was coming down the pike. There have been months to do this, and I don’t think anyone is saying don’t reauthorize at all. The argument is this is an incredibly powerful surveillance tool, and there needs to be guardrails in place to protect people’s constitutional rights.” Himes, arguably the Democratic Party’s biggest champion of FISA, seems willing to give Trump one more win before the blue wave crashes down in Washington. “I made it clear to some very senior administration officials that they should get this thing done in the lame-duck,” he told The Hill, “because it’s, you know, going to be a very different 702 that gets reauthorized in the first quarter of next year.” But Himes didn’t have the votes this summer, and it’s even less likely that he’ll have the votes for a clean reauthorization now.

articles.title: Jensen Huang reportedly tells Nvidia staff it’s ‘not true’ Trump got him rehired
articles.summary: Jensen Huang apologized to staff during his first all-hands since returning as CEO, saying he wasn’t reinstated because of pressure from President Trump or because of “tech bro” culture.
articles.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to staff during his first all-hands since returning to the company, while attempting to distance himself from the narrative that the White House and tech leaders helped him get his job back, according to reports from Bloomberg, The New York Times, and The Handbasket’s Marisa Kabas. During the meeting, Huang reportedly called claims that President Donald Trump was directly involved in his reinstatement — an idea publicly promoted by Trump himself — “completely untrue.” He added, “Don’t think for a second politics played a role in the company. We are the most apolitical company,” according to Kabas. Along with attempting to dismiss Trump’s involvement, Huang reportedly said he also didn’t return because he was a “tech bro” who was “above the law” or “above the code of conduct.” He added that, “no story has been more tortured than this one in human history,” Kabas reports. Instead, Huang said the Nvidia board “evaluated the entire situation,” while receiving assurance from the government that he posed no national security threat, according to the NYT. Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on November 12th, following reports of affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two employees, including vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell. On Monday, Nvidia announced that it had reinstated Huang as CEO, president, and member of the board — a decision the White House said Trump was “totally involved in.” Trump also confirmed that he worked with Vice President JD Vance and other officials to bring Huang back. A swath of tech leaders, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and former White House AI czar David Sacks, were also in favor of Huang’s return. In a post on Truth Social, Trump said that the government “has no reason to believe” Huang’s return poses a risk to national security, adding that the US attorney general “does not possess evidence” that he engaged in “unlawful conduct.” Nvidia is still facing an investigation over its accounting practices, according to Reuters. The company is also carrying out its own internal investigation surrounding reports that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy plot. Huang is set to testify before Congress on December 1st to answer questions about national security concerns, and Democrats are already planning to press Huang about his return, as well as Trump’s involvement. Even after all this, Huang reportedly said he “doesn’t believe in succession planning.” He also acknowledged that he violated Nvidia’s code of conduct, adding that he is attending therapy daily, Bloomberg reports. “I made some terrible mistakes,” Huang said, according to the NYT. “I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids and of course, I hurt all of you.”

articles.title: Army set to detonate lead munitions in Iowa: What to know
articles.summary: The Army is poised to detonate lead-containing weapons in Iowa on Wednesday, sending a burst of lead dust into the air. The controlled destruction of the munitions has been highly controversial, both over potential health risks and how the issue advanced to this situation in the first place. Here’s what the public needs to know:…
articles.body:
The Army is poised to detonate lead-containing weapons in Iowa on Wednesday, sending a burst of lead dust into the air.

The controlled destruction of the munitions has been highly controversial, both over potential health risks and how the issue advanced to this situation in the first place.

At around 9 a.m. local time on Wednesday, the Army is expected to explode lead azide munitions at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. This is expected to send up a plume of lead-containing particles.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The latest map from the Army indicates that the plume could travel in a southwest direction.

Officials say they will take measures aimed at mitigating the impacts of the explosion, including using a water wall to absorb the blast impact and associated pollution.

Lead azide munitions appear to have been at the site for a long time. A 2014 press release references a research project happening in response to “concerns over a 40-year-old stockpile of lead azide deteriorating at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa.”

The Army has said, meanwhile, that it “uncovered” the degrading lead azide in March. It said that “it was determined that a controlled detonation was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area.”

Officials say that they need to dispose of the lead azide, an explosive used in detonators that’s currently being stored in 68 plastic drums, in a controlled way in order to prevent an accidental explosion that could have greater consequences.

Army Col. Aaron Teller said in a court filing that in April, the Army inspected the drums and found crystallization in 58 of them. He said the lids of the barrels where they are kept are “no longer safe to remove because of unknown crystal growth” meaning they cannot be refilled with a water and ethanol mixture that was being used to keep the lead azide stable.

Without that mixture, he said in court, the munitions are “more susceptible to freezing which can increase sensitivity of the crystals and cause an uncontrolled detonation.”

Teller warned against allowing the munitions to explode accidentally because “an uncontrolled detonation can result in an incomplete destruction of the lead azide during the explosion, causing both the potential for secondary explosive events and an extremely unsafe condition for personnel conducting post-blast cleanup activities. Incomplete destruction of the lead azide during an uncontrolled explosion may also cause unpredictable dispersal of the explosive material, leading to an ongoing explosives safety issue in the impacted area.”

While the government says the controlled detonation is the best way to go at this point, critics say the issue is a mess of the Army’s own making.

Rachel Rintelmann, managing attorney at Earthjustice, said that the key question is: “Why are we in this situation in the first place?”

“This may be an emergency now, but it is an emergency of the Army’s creation,” Rintelmann said. “It is their mismanagement of this hazardous waste and their allowing it to deteriorate to this point that has put us in this crisis now.”

What are the health impacts of lead exposure?

Lead is a neurotoxin and is particularly harmful to babies and children.

Exposure to lead in children can cause brain damage, nervous system damage, learning problems, behavioral issues and a lower IQ. In rare cases, it can also cause seizures, coma and death, according to the Environmental Protection Agency .

In adults, lead exposure can cause decreased kidney function, heart-related issues and fertility issues.

Lead exposure can also harm a developing fetus. In pregnant women, exposure can cause early birth or low birth weight, harm fetal development, and increase the risk of a miscarriage or stillbirth.

“Lead doesn’t break down into something else; it just is lead. And so, if that dust gets transported through the air, wherever it lands … it will be there for some time, so … that means it’s going to be a longer-term exposure,” Peter DeCarlo, a professor who studies air pollution at Johns Hopkins University recently told The Hill .

“One of the things we worry about sometimes is if this dust can get into a home and it’s no longer airborne, but it’s on the ground … then it’s particularly potentially problematic for little kids who play on the floor and who are more prone to putting their hands in their mouth,” DeCarlo said.

The latest Army advisory recommends relocation of “all residents of Middletown, Iowa, and immediate surrounding impacted areas” which includes a 5-mile cone extending southwest.

In a press briefing Wednesday, a key Department of Health and Human Services official particularly emphasized that children, pregnant women and chronically ill people should leave the area.

The Army said that residents outside the evacuation zone should shelter in place.

“Best practices include closing all windows and doors, setting heating to recirculate … turning off fans that pull in outside air … keeping small children and pets inside, and covering feed and water for livestock and crops,” the advisory states.

Illinois state officials have said that potentially impacted residents should stay inside by keeping doors and windows closed for 24 to 48 hours.

But the detonation is occurring the day before Thanksgiving, a holiday in which people frequently travel to each other’s homes.

President Trump this week backed the detonation but also sought to leave it in the hands of Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D).

In a Monday post on Truth Social, Trump wrote, “I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation.”

“If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation,” the president added.

In response, Sand passed the issue back to the Trump administration.

“The Administration should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks,” he wrote on social media Monday.

Sand also called for the federal government to share more information with the public.

Current Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds (R) wrote Tuesday on social platform X, “I take the Army’s warning seriously that the choice is between a planned detonation and an uncontrolled explosion.”

“I believe, based on the information I’ve been given, that the danger is immediate, and I trust the Army will do everything in its power to protect the people who could be affected,” she added.

Iowa Sen. Chuck Grassley (R) has said in a statement that “a controlled, safe removal of the lead azide far outweighs a spontaneous catastrophe.”

Fellow Iowa Sen. Joni Ernst (R) said, “I understand the real risks of further delaying this controlled detonation. I support every effort to reduce the risk of lead exposure to the public.”

images.caption: A sign hangs from a fence surrounding the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Nov. 23, 2026, in Middletown, Iowa. Middletown is preparing for the Army to detonate several tons of highly volatile, degraded lead azide at the facility. The detonation was scheduled to take place on Nov. 20 but following an outpouring of public concern about the environmental impact, it had been postponed awaiting a court ruling.

articles.title: Dozens of oil and shipping tankers hacked in recent weeks, per report | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Iran is the chief suspect behind the dozens of cyberattacks targeting oil and chemical shipping vessels.
articles.body:
U.S. officials suspect Iranian hackers may be behind as many as 50 cyberattacks targeting shipping vessels in recent weeks, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal .

The ships carrying oil, liquefied gas, and other explosive chemicals were hacked as they traveled across Asia and Europe. Several oil tankers headed toward the U.S. coast in August also had their navigation systems breached, prompting cybersecurity teams within the FBI and Coast Guard to board the vessels.

The report said officials are investigating if Iran is expanding its recent wave of hacks against the U.S. by targeting large vessels to sow fear among shippers, disrupt routes, or to cause an explosion at a port. (Ships have backup controls in the event that automated systems are hacked or fail.)

Hackers may have been abusing a bug dubbed FortiBleed , which allows hackers to break into networks by compromising vulnerable Fortinet-made routers. A joint FBI-Coast Guard security alert from September warned that Fortinet routers are used on shipping vessels.

Iran has been firing back on all sides since the start of the U.S./Israel-led war earlier this year, which killed the country’s supreme leader. Many of Iran’s retaliations have been in the form of cyberattacks, with U.S. officials blaming Iran for hacks targeting hundreds of American water providers and U.S. medical tech companies .

A spokesperson for the FBI did not respond to a request for comment about the shipping hacks or whether it had a more accurate figure.

articles.title: Navy says it won’t rename USS Doris Miller aircraft carrier after Trump
articles.summary: The Navy says it has “no intention” of changing the name of the USS Doris Miller, meant to honor a Black World War II war hero, following public outcry over a reported plan to possibly rename the aircraft carrier after President Trump. “There is no intention to change the name of the USS Doris Miller,”…
articles.body:
The Navy says it has “no intention” of changing the name of the USS Doris Miller, meant to honor a Black World War II war hero, following public outcry over a reported plan to possibly rename the aircraft carrier after President Trump.

“There is no intention to change the name of the USS Doris Miller,” a Ford-class aircraft carrier currently under construction in Virginia, according to a Navy statement released to media outlets last week.

Doris Miller, a Black sailor honored for his heroism at Pearl Harbor, served aboard the battleship USS West Virginia as a cook when Japanese forces attacked Pearl Harbor on Dec. 7, 1941. Miller quickly jumped to help wounded sailors before manning an antiaircraft gun and firing at Japanese planes, despite having no formal training on the weapon, taking down at least one aircraft.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The new carrier received its name in 2020 during a ceremony at Pearl Harbor — during Trump’s first term — marking the first such vessel to carry the name of a Black American, as well as the first named in honor of a sailor’s actions performed while serving in the enlisted ranks.

But CNN first reported in August that the Navy was considering renaming the ship, with conversations including naming it for Trump. One source told the outlet that the service had even stopped using Miller’s name to refer to the vessel, instead internally mentioning it by its hull number, CVN-81.

The report quickly sparked outrage, with 73 House members writing a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao urging them to “reject this plan and ensure that CVN-81 bears the name USS Doris Miller.”

Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) then introduced three bills intended to prevent a name change, including one to bar naming any Navy ship for a sitting president or vice president.

Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) in October went a step further when she introduced similar legislation that would prevent naming any Defense Department asset, not just ships, for a sitting president.

There is no federal law currently barring Navy vessels from being named after a sitting commander in chief, but doing so would break long-standing tradition.

NAACP President Derrick Johnson at the time called the alleged talks around the change “ a slap in the face to every war hero and to every service member who has worn the uniform.”

Newport News Shipbuilding is set to lay the ship’s ceremonial keel Dec. 5, two days ahead of the 85th anniversary of the attack on Pearl Harbor.

images.caption: Family members of World War II hero Doris “Dorie” Miller react after the unveiling of the new Ford-class aircraft carrier USS Doris Miller (CVN-81) at a Martin Luther King Day celebration event on Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam. This will be the second ship named in honor of Miller, and the first aircraft carrier ever named for an African American and an enlisted Sailor.

articles.title: Maple raises $5.3M to build AI products that protect your data, even from itself | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The startup's encrypted AI architecture is designed to prevent even the company itself from accessing users' private data.
articles.body:
As AI assistants evolve into more capable agents that can access our files, emails, calendar, browser, and more, the amount of trust we’re expected to place in AI companies is growing. One startup called Maple , co-founded by a former Apple engineer who worked on privacy-preserving technologies, is taking a different approach with its AI app, where users’ data remains private — even from the company itself.

“We wanted to build something that was not only encrypted but also could be proven, and that people could go look at the open-source code, and then they could look at what we call trusted execution environments,” explains Maple co-founder and CEO Mark Suman . “They can look at and verify the code that’s running on our servers, so they don’t really have to take our word for it.”

“They can audit everything themselves and know how their data is being handled,” he adds.

The idea of trust is Maple’s larger theme, as the startup proposes that there’s a way to build an AI app where consumers don’t have to trade privacy for convenience, as its competitors often require with their invasive privacy policies , data collection practices , and sometimes even training on users’ personal data .

Instead of asking users to trust that Maple won’t misuse their personal data, it’s attempting to build a business where it can’t access that data in the first place.

Like other AI apps on the market, Maple allows users to engage in a chat experience where they ask questions and get answers. Meanwhile, its newly launched desktop app, Maple Work , offers a more agentic experience where the AI can control your computer, work with your files and apps, and control your browser to get online tasks handled.

With the company’s recently closed $5.3 million round, it’s moving on to its next product — a cloud-based agent that will be able to continue its work even if your computer isn’t on. This addition would make Maple more competitive with other popular consumer AI services, like Meta’s Muse , Instinct , and other AI agents that work over chat.

The oversubscribed seed round was led by EPIC Ventures, with participation from Draper Associates, Planetary VC, and Epoch VC, and follows a pre-seed angel round of under a million. Maple plans to raise a Series A in the first half of 2027, given the investor interest.

Suman, who previously spent six years at Apple, already had a background where AI and privacy overlapped, he tells TechCrunch.

At Apple, he worked on AI and machine learning with a particular focus on computer vision. Given Apple’s stance on consumer privacy, the challenge he faced was building products that would protect people’s identity while benefiting from computer vision techniques. His co-founder, Anthony Ronning (CTO), has a background in defense tech, security, and networking.

Ronning started the company that later became Maple AI back in 2023, initially as a privacy-focused fintech. When Suman teamed up with Ronning in August 2024, the idea to create Maple AI was born. The following January, the product became available to the public as a mobile app.

The app offers a familiar interface for those used to AI chatbots, but under the hood it runs a variety of open models, including versions of DeepSeek , Kimi , GLM , Inkling from Thinking Machines, Google’s Gemma , and OpenAI’s GPT OSS . Users can pick and choose the models they want or, for a simpler experience, just toggle between a quick model and the more powerful one.

The models themselves run inside a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) — meaning a server with hardware encryption on it — within a U.S.-based data center. (Maple also offers support for European customers through a partner that runs its server in Europe).

“We actually don’t have access to [the data] while it’s inside the TEE,” explains Suman. “The data gets encrypted first on your device using a unique password that’s only known by you, the user — we don’t have access to it. It then goes into this TEE, and it gets decrypted inside there. The AI does its thing, and then it re-encrypts it with your password and sends it back to you,” he continues. “So we provide an end-to-end experience that’s very easy for the user, but we actually don’t have access to the raw data as it’s in flight or even when it’s at rest,” he adds.

This allows Maple to protect its users’ data, even from outsiders — like if hackers breached its system or the government came with a subpoena, for instance. All it could do would be to hand over an encrypted file.

“We just simply don’t want access to it,” Suman says of customers’ data. “That’s not part of our business model. And we also don’t want it to be part of our threat model.”

With the new desktop app, Maple is looking to small businesses who may want to benefit from AI without the data privacy risks. Inside the app, there’s an integration store where users can connect with other apps, like their Gmail or calendar. The desktop app can also spin up a subagent that works inside another AI app you may have on your desktop, like Claude, Codex, or others that support the Agent Client Protocol (ACP). This allows customers to use their preferred AI app for specific tasks, without having to give it all their information — just what’s needed for the given task.

Next year, Maple plans to enter the enterprise market with pilot work, where it will offer its own version of zero data retention. (Maple doesn’t retain most of the customers’ data, but when it has to, that data is encrypted.) It’s now in the process of completing SOC 2 compliance and security audits to get ready for this expansion.

The company declined to share its registered customer numbers, but noted it’s seen 60x growth over the past three months, as people have been looking for ways to increase their security with AI.

Maple currently generates revenue via subscriptions, which are comparable to those from other AI model providers. Its Pro plan is $20 per month, and it offers two Max plans, Max and Max Plus, at $100 and $200 per month, respectively.

The Austin- and San Francisco-based startup is a team of four and is actively hiring.

articles.title: Newborn hepatitis B vaccination rates dropped sharply after RFK Jr.-led confusion
articles.summary: Far fewer newborns are being vaccinated against hepatitis B, according to a new study, as parents continue to reject an immunization once considered routine. The rate of infants who received the hepatitis B Virus (HBV) vaccine fell to 65.6 percent in 2026, down from around 80 percent from 2020 to 2022, according to a study…
articles.body:
Far fewer newborns are being vaccinated against hepatitis B, according to a new study, as parents continue to reject an immunization once considered routine.

The rate of infants who received the hepatitis B Virus (HBV) vaccine fell to 65.6 percent in 2026, down from around 80 percent from 2020 to 2022, according to a study published Tuesday in The New England Journal of Medicine.

The birth dose protects infants against hepatitis B infection and can serve as a safety net for babies of mothers who don’t know they’re infected with the virus and unknowingly transmit it during childbirth.

The research was based on data from Truveta, a healthcare and analytics company, which included health information on 140 million people in the U.S.

The researchers analyzed more than 1.3 million infants born between January 2018 through June 2026 and found that newborn HBV vaccination rates increased from 76 percent in 2018 to 80 percent in 2022 before declining in mid-2023.

But the drop off accelerated substantially after Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. took office, and his reconstituted vaccine advisory panel overhauled the childhood vaccine schedule.

The study findings likely reflect “continuing vaccine hesitancy and confusion among parents after recent changes in recommendations for newborn HBV guidelines,” the researchers wrote.

Dr. Nina Masters, one of the study’s authors and a principal applied research scientist at Truveta, called the shift “substantial.”

“This decline really outpaces the decline that we saw for other vaccines, so it was a bit shocking to see just how far vaccination rates have fallen,” Masters said.

The study follows a decision from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s (CDC) vaccine advisory panel at the end of last year to reverse its universal recommendation for HBV at birth, which has been in place since 1991.

On Dec. 5, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) issued a new recommendation that parents consult with a doctor about whether or not their child needs this shot within the first 24 hours after birth if the mother does not test positive for HBV.

The panel and its recommendations are tied up in court, but the recommendations sowed confusion among parents.

“We can surmise that there’s a lot of vaccine hesitancy out there,” Masters said.

While ACIP’s new advisory still recommends vaccination for infants whose mothers test positive for HBV, the study found that there was also a drop-off in HBV immunizations among this population this year.

Vaccination for children born to HBV-positive mothers fell from between approximately 97 to 98 percent from 2020 to 2025 to 93.9 percent in 2026.

The long-term effects of this declining vaccination rate remain to be seen. HBV spreads through contact with infected blood and can cause acute or chronic liver infection.

Around 640,000 people in the U.S. who are 20 years or older are living with chronic, or long-term, hepatitis B, according to a CDC estimate earlier this month. If untreated, this virus can cause liver damage, cirrhosis, cancer and death.

“This birth dose hepatitis B vaccination is really a safety net,” Masters said. “If the mother is infected with hepatitis B, it’s very effective at preventing perinatal transmission, and if that infant does get perinatally infected with hepatitis B, there’s a strong chance of chronic hepatitis B infection.”

Cases of acute hepatitis B fell dramatically in children after the CDC began recommending a universal birth dose in 1991 — falling 99 percent from 1990 to 2019.

The report falls across a backdrop of vaccine skepticism that has also been tied to rising measles cases in the country this year in states like Texas, New Mexico, New York, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin.

The CDC reports there have been 5,838 confirmed measles cases in the U.S. this year — more than double the number reported last year. The U.S. lost its measles elimination status , a distinction it has maintained since 2000 , after experiencing 12 months of sustained domestic transmission.

articles.title: Huang apologizes to Nvidia employees, says he’s in therapy: Reports
articles.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to the company and admitted he was in therapy every day in his first all-hands meeting with employees since he was reinstated, according to new reports. “I made some terrible mistakes,” Huang told employees, adding that he was unfaithful to his wife, The New York Times reported. “I hurt my kids…
articles.body:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to the company and admitted he was in therapy every day in his first all-hands meeting with employees since he was reinstated , according to new reports.

“I made some terrible mistakes,” Huang told employees, adding that he was unfaithful to his wife, The New York Times reported. “I hurt my kids and of course, hurt all of you.”

He revealed he was in mental health therapy every day for 90 minutes and that it was helping him “a lot,” per Wired, citing remarks it reviewed. He continued to say that it was “not acceptable” that he violated Nvidia’s code of conduct.

Huang is referring to allegations that he engaged in an extramarital affair with a woman who U.S. officials suspected was a Chinese intelligence asset, along with reportedly having relationships with two other Nvidia employees. Nvidia encouraged employees to “avoid situations where our actions create conflict,” which included personal relationships, according to its code of conduct .

During the call, Huang disputed allegations that President Trump and other high-level administration officials were involved in his rehiring, saying, “That is also completely untrue,” the Times and Wired reported.

He stated he was back because Nvidia’s board of directors “evaluated the entire situation” and “gathered facts” after also receiving assurances from the Trump administration that Huang wasn’t a national security threat.

“It is absolutely true that President Trump really, really loves our company,” Huang expressed, per Wired. “He gloats about Nvidia. You know he does.”

“But there’s a question about politics. Are we now political? Are we partisan? I wanna be very clear with you. President Trump is the United States president. He is my president,” he continued. “And I’ll do everything I can to help this president be informed about how he could make decisions that are in the best interest of our country.”

Trump has been a staunch and vocal supporter of the tech leader after he was ousted from the company earlier this month. He called on Nvidia multiple times to reinstate Huang, though The Hill previously reported the board wasn’t weighing this proposal.

When Nvidia reversed course on Huang, Trump boasted in a lengthy CNBC interview Monday that he had “been speaking to the board directly and indirectly.”

“I felt very strongly about it. And I felt more strongly as I saw what was happening with the company, because that was to me, a very important part of our country,” the president said.

The Hill recently reported that Vice President Vance was personally involved in Trump’s push to reinstate Huang over the weekend, according to a source familiar with the matter.

Nvidia did not respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment.

articles.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets
articles.summary: A federal jury found the Chinese telecom giant Huawei guilty of stealing trade secrets.
articles.body: A jury has found Huawei guilty of stealing US trade secrets, as reported earlier by NBC News and Bloomberg. The verdict, handed down in a federal court in New York, concludes a years-long legal battle that accused the Chinese telecom giant of stealing source code and proprietary technology from several companies, including T-Mobile, Cisco, and Motorola. The Department of Justice’s 2018 criminal indictment against Huawei came to light following the arrest of the company’s CFO, Wanzhou Meng, whom the agency accused of fraud. Though the indictment against Meng was eventually dismissed, she admitted to misleading banks over Huawei’s operations in Iran as part of a deferred prosecution agreement. The US government blacklisted Huawei in 2019 over national security concerns. In total, the jury found Huawei guilty of 10 of 12 criminal counts, including money laundering, violating US sanctions, bank fraud, wire fraud, and conspiracy to defraud the US. The company was acquitted of engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy and obstruction of justice. Huawei’s sentencing is set for September 14th, 2027, where it may face “financial penalties including criminal fines, forfeiture, and restitution,” according to the DOJ. “For over two decades, Huawei built its global empire on a foundation of fraud, theft, and deception,” Tysen A. Duva, the assistant attorney general of the DOJ’s criminal division, says in a statement. “Huawei’s crimes threatened the U.S. financial system, took advantage of American companies that compete honestly in the global telecommunications market, and undermined our national security.” In a statement to NBC News, a Huawei spokesperson said the charges are “without legal or factual merit” and that it plans to appeal the decision. Huawei didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment. Update, November 24th: Added information from the DOJ.

articles.title: Nearly 1 in 3 Americans have ‘very little’ faith in FAA: Poll
articles.summary: Nearly a third of Americans have “very little” faith in the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), according to a new survey. In The Economist/YouGov poll, 28 percent of respondents said they have “very little” confidence in the FAA, while 44 percent said they have “some” and 19 percent said they have “quite a lot.” Nine percent…
articles.body:
Nearly a third of Americans have “very little” faith in the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), according to a new survey.

In The Economist/YouGov poll , 28 percent of respondents said they have “very little” confidence in the FAA, while 44 percent said they have “some” and 19 percent said they have “quite a lot.” Nine percent of those surveyed said they have “a great deal” of confidence in the agency.

The poll, which took place from Friday to Monday, comes after the FAA ordered an hours-long nationwide ground stop earlier in November. The FAA pointed to a router in Arkansas and a Texas-based radar site as the two probable reasons behind the outage.

On Tuesday, President Trump advised travelers of “slow motion” air traffic before the Thanksgiving holiday week.

“For those traveling on the roads this holiday season, as you know, we have a very antiquated system, and we’re going to rebuild it for the airports,” Trump said.

“The air traffic control is 57 years old. That’s like some of the younger parts of it. But we’re going to be getting the money, hopefully, from Congress so we’ll be able to build it, and we’ll end up with the best air traffic,” the president continued.

The FAA wrote on social media Tuesday evening that a ground stop had been lifted at Chicago O’Hare International Airport, but the agency was “temporarily delaying some flights while technicians work to repair a piece of air traffic equipment.”

“The issue is specific to O’Hare, and it does not impact all flights nor affect any other airports or FAA systems,” the agency added.

In The Economist/YouGov poll, 25 percent of respondents called the “overall safety record” of American airline travel “excellent,” compared to 48 percent who rated it “good” and 20 percent who said “only fair.” Six percent of those surveyed rated U.S. airline travel’s overall safety record as “poor.”

The Economist/YouGov poll featured 1,623 respondents and a margin of error of 2.9 percentage points.

articles.body:
President Trump’s successful effort to pressure Nvidia’s board to bring back Jensen Huang as CEO has sparked a furious reaction from lawmakers in both parties, promising to make the relationship between the two men a central point of congressional investigations.

The ramped-up oversight of Trump and Jensen Huang, who lost his job after reports of separate affairs with a subordinate and an alleged Chinese spy, will begin next week when the CEO appears for a closed-door transcribed interview with three House panels on Dec. 1 and public testimony before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

It is also likely to bolster congressional efforts to pass stronger export controls on chip manufacturing.

“The momentum has clearly shifted,” said Brendan Steinhauser, a Republican strategist and CEO of The Alliance for Secure AI.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), the ranking member of the Senate Banking Committee who likely will become the panel’s chair in January, said Jensen Huang’s reinstatement “only increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law.”

Lawmakers who want tougher export controls are focused on making additions to the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), a defense policy bill that has been approved every year by Congress for decades. Lawmakers are expected to make a push to pass it in the lame-duck session, though they face various challenges.

“I would probably put the 50-50 probability, or maybe higher than 50-50 that the export controls get passed through the NDAA in a bipartisan fashion,” said Steinhauser.

The bills would allow Congress to block advanced AI chip exports to U.S. foreign adversaries, block the sale of essential chipmaking tools to countries of concern, and would require AI chips subject to export controls to have a “location verification mechanism,” respectively.

Trump and his administration have maintained there is no evidence that Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia poses a national security risk to the U.S.

But lawmakers have voiced a plethora of concerns, including whether national security was compromised in an effort to sell advanced chips to China.

Steinhauser argued the White House should embrace the bills.

“They can still say that they want Jensen at the top of the Nvidia, but also say they want to make sure that the chips don’t go to China, that we pass the Chips Security Act, the MATCH [Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware] Act, and the Overwatch Act to protect America’s national security, and prevent the Chinese from building on our technology stack and getting closer to keeping up with us.”

The Commerce Department has come under scrutiny after reports surfaced that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick took a softer approach to Nvidia over its AI chip sales to China and did not put the Singaporean firm Megaspeed on the trade entity blacklist.

Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials suspect of passing information to Beijing while reportedly having an affair with Jensen Huang, is a former Megaspeed executive.

“The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” Warren said in a statement Monday.

Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.), who also sits on the Banking panel, echoed the point in an interview with Bloomberg on Tuesday.

“This also absolutely reinforces what I and a number of other members of the Senate have been saying, which is we need more legislation to restrict the export of these most advanced chips,” McCormick told the outlet.

“I think this gives additional momentum to those legislative efforts,” he continued.

McCormick also warned of what he said was a “slippery slope” of the government getting involved in the governance of private corporations.

“I am worried about the precedent of the executive branch getting involved in really ownership deals with companies but also in board governance and making these decisions,” McCormick said.

John Ullyot, former deputy assistant to Trump and National Security Council spokesperson during the first Trump administration, likened the practice of government intervention in private companies to China.

“We also need to watch out whenever Washington starts telling companies how to run their business. That sounds a lot more like China than America,” he said.

Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.), another Banking Committee member, said he expects Jensen Huang to plead the Fifth.

“It is my place to tell him that if you’re cheating on your wife with somebody who could be a Chinese spy, that jeopardizes national security,” Kennedy said.

Jensen Huang was reinstated to his post after an aggressive push from Trump, Vice President Vance and other members of the administration over the weekend.

“I think it was rushed, and I think that this makes me feel like any investigation they do internally will not be anything other than a whitewash,” Steinhauser said of Nvidia’s investigation.

“The most concerning thing I think is national security implications,” he said. “But again, if they would have waited, done the investigation, gone before Congress, testified and it all came out that, OK, this is really more of a major HR [human resources] issue, then OK, the company can handle it as they see fit.”

When announcing his return, the Nvidia board said Monday that it “believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.”

“We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company,” Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s board chair, said in a statement Monday.

The board said it received input from “senior levels” of the U.S. government, giving it confidence that his reinstatement poses no national security risk. But it also said it would be continuing its own investigation.

“Trump gave them immunity. So that seems to be the key factor,” said Darrell West, a senior fellow from the Brookings Institute. “The board caved to presidential pressure.”

West said there are national security and investigation risks with Jensen Huang’s reinstatement.

“The company is taking a big risk in terms of what could be revealed,” he said. “There could be more disclosures that come out that are embarrassing for the company.”

Both West and Steinhauser said they expect Congress to ask the appropriate questions to Jensen Huang despite his reinstatement.

“I do think they will ask tough questions,” Steinhauser said. “I think they want to get to the bottom of all of this. I do think members of Congress will try and hold them accountable, but I don’t think you’ll see that from the White House.”

West said that the China hawks in both parties will press Jensen Huang on the questions they have.

“There has already been leading people in Congress who have expressed astonishment at this and a renewed willingness to get to the bottom of it,” he said.
